#6705. Australia, Through the Eyes of Its Traditional Custodians

In the Kimberley, in Australia’s far northwest, land and human history are inextricably linked and almost incomprehensibly ancient. Its sandstone ranges, built from rock up to 1.8 billion years old, are almost half the age of the Earth itself. Close to the shores of Warrabii (Swift Bay), inside a cave carved from that ancient stone, are paintings of stenciled hands dating back an estimated 20,000 years. Lying on your back to look up at them feels like a living link to the person who made them—blowing a mix of ochre, water, and animal fat over a hand pressed to the rock—a portal through time to Aboriginal Australia, the world’s oldest continuous living culture, stretching back at least 65,000 years.

Bardi Jawi artist Bruce Wiggan at work at Cygnet Bay Pearl Farm, where he carves riji: pearl shell engraved with geometric or figurative designs, the grooves then rubbed with ochre or charcoal mixed with resin or fat.

A riji in progress on Wiggan’s workbench. Engraved pearl shell has long been a highly prized trade item, passed along routes that stretched from the Kimberley to central and southern Australia.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, who comprise hundreds of language groups, each with its own distinct culture and law, hold an unparalleled understanding of Country. Capitalized in Aboriginal English, the word encompasses far more than a physical space. As the Gay’wu Group of Women write in Songspirals: Sharing Women’s Wisdom of Country Through Songlines, “To talk of Country means not just land, but also the waters, the people, the winds, animals, plants, stories, songs, and feelings, everything that becomes together to make up place. Country is alive for us—it cares for us, communicates with us, and we are part of it.”

Navigating the waterways of the Kimberley between sandstone walls laid down some 1.8 billion years ago, on a coast where the tides can swing more than 11 meters.

Yet the fabric of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander societies was torn and could have been lost forever. After the British invaded the shores of what is now Australia in 1788, they set about colonizing its people and Country. The continent’s First Peoples were enslaved, massacred, and displaced. Between 1910 and 1970, as many as one in three Indigenous children, tens of thousands in total, were forcibly removed from their families and placed in government- and church-run institutions, forbidden from speaking their languages or practicing their cultures. They became known as the Stolen Generations. More recently, in 2023, Australians voted against enshrining an Indigenous Voice to Parliament, an advisory body that would have given First Nations people a formal say on the decisions that affect them.

Indigenous resilience and determination have ensured this is also a story of endurance and restoration. Through native title and land rights, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples’ connection to their traditional lands and waters is now legally recognized across more than half of Australia, though rarely as full ownership. Truth-telling processes, which build an official public record of historical and ongoing injustice, are underway in several states; in late 2025, Victoria signed the nation’s first treaty with its First Peoples.

Indigenous-led tourism is growing fast too: more than 1.25 million international visitors took part in an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander experience last year, contributing an estimated $450 million to the economy across more than 2,500 Indigenous-owned businesses. Every one of those bookings is an act: to experience Country as a guest, through the eyes of its Traditional Custodians, and to put money directly into community-led hands rather than extractive, colonial models of travel.

A hand-painted sign welcomes visitors to Murdudjurl, the Murumburr family community on the edge of the Jim Jim Creek, home to Mandy Muir and her mother, Elder Jessie Alderson.

What follows are the voices of seven Custodians, each speaking for their own Country.

Mandy Muir is a senior Murumburr custodian and Kakadu National Park’s longest-serving guide, leading tours on Yellow Water Billabong and at the Burrungkuy rock art site in the Northern Territory. Her family runs Kakadu Billabong Safari Camp on the Jim Jim Creek system—carrying forward more than 65,000 years of continuous Bininj culture.

Mandy Muir, a senior custodian of the Murumburr clan, holds a freshly picked andem, or waterlily, on the banks of Jim Jim Creek, before preparing the plant's tubers to eat.

“Language is what ties us to this Country—it’s how my mob and I know exactly who we are and where we belong. I grew up here in the park, one of 36 kids at the little school when it first opened, learning the European curriculum in the classroom, then going out with elders each week to learn about Country.

Muir’s grandson fishes on Jim Jim Creek near her home, where the fresh tracks of a basking crocodile are pressed into the sand at his feet.

Our calendar follows the stars, and the cycles of animals, plants, and water. When andem (pink waterlilies) flower on the billabong during Yekke and Wurrkeng, our cooler dry months, it’s an important bush food: the tubers and seeds, mabala, eaten raw or cooked, or ground into flour for bush bread, along with the young flower stems, anbardmo. The yellow Andjedji flowers that bloom around the same time tell us Kumoken (freshwater crocodiles) are laying eggs on the sandy creek banks.

My family still weaves jewelry from kunngobarn (pandanus), harvested fresh from the bush with a manmarli (hooked stick), then dried and dyed with roots, berries, and flowers. It’s long been Women’s Business: a time to sit together, share stories, sip tea, and pass knowledge down through daughters, aunties, and grandmothers.

Muir’s cousin makes handwoven pandanus jewelry from materials gathered in the surrounding bush.

At home, while my nephew and I prepare a bush barbecue, my son and daughter paint rarrk—the cross-hatching we use in ceremony, once painted onto bodies to encode our stories and our connection to land, kin, and the Dreaming.

The sun sets over a Kakadu floodplain. In the Top End’s dry season, sunsets like this are almost a daily event, as dust and fine particles carried on dry southeasterly winds scatter the low evening light into deep reds and oranges.

This escarpment Country is home to animals found nowhere else on Earth, like the Oenpelli python and the black wallaroo. This river system, these wetlands, the crocodiles we live alongside (the park is home to around 10,000 of them) are part of our story and our responsibility. When we burn Country, it’s about rejuvenating the land and bringing food back for animals, the way our ancestors did.

Guests at Kakadu Billabong Safari Camp, owned by Mandy Muir, wake to still morning reflections on the billabong, in the heart of crocodile country.

But the climate is changing fast, and Burrungkuy’s rock art—20,000 years old, depicting everything from creation stories to environmental and social change—is deteriorating. If people don’t start listening to the land and the knowledge holders, we risk losing not only our home but our cultural heritage.”

On the beaches of Broome, Patricia Torres—a Djugun, Yawuru, Ngumbarl, Jabirr-Jabirr, Nyul-Nyul, and Bard woman, elder, writer, and bush tucker guide—reads the coastline as a living archive. Founder of Jarndu Ngaank Tours and Mayi Harvests, a native-food enterprise, and now a philosophy doctorate student, she speaks about what colonization took from her people, and what it will take to give it back.

Djugun Elder Patricia Torres holds a hand-painted baler shell during a Welcome to Country, a ceremony in which Traditional Owners welcome visitors to their land.

“When I stand here on this coast, every element carries a story: the plants we use to heal jellyfish stings and reef cuts, the tides that race out for miles, exposing 130-million-year-old dinosaur footprints at Gantheaume Point. Our people read land and water so closely that even the call of a small yellow-breasted bird was a warning—time to go—knowledge that kept us alive for generations.

This coastline once held thick mangroves—our defense against erosion, nurseries for fish and crabs. During the pearling boom, many were cleared for more boats and profit. From the early slave raids through that boom, my own ancestors were among those kidnapped off this coast, forced into pearling labor, and criminalized when they resisted.

Colonization didn’t stop at land and lives: it took our stories, designs, plants, even our identities. Today our motifs and native foods are used as branding by people who aren’t us, while we’re locked out of the wealth it creates—what we call black cladding. Our children and men are over-policed and over-imprisoned, often asked to leave their ways of knowing at school.

Yet our culture is profoundly sophisticated. We lit small controlled fires to hunt, clear pathways, and stop wildfires spreading—practices that kept Country healthy. Our flood stories remember the sea rising and swallowing land thousands of years before Western science could prove it; geologists have since matched them to the exact sea-level changes after the last ice age.

North of Broome, the red pindan country of the Dampier Peninsula gives way to salt flats and mangrove-lined tidal creeks fed by the Indian Ocean.

My work is about truth-telling and decolonizing the mind. By the 1970s, anthropologists had written the Djugun and Jabirr Jabirr off as ‘virtually extinct.’ After eight generations of dispossession, we are still here—that, for me, is decolonization: restoring truth, renewing our relationship to Country, and making sure our children feel powerful, connected, and fully seen.”

Out of Cygnet Bay Pearl Farm at Borrgoron, on the tip of the Dampier Peninsula, Terry Hunter runs Borrgoron Coast to Creek Tours, sharing 40,000 years of Bardi connection to this coastline. Descended from both a notorious enslaver, Harry Hunter, and those he enslaved, Hunter reconciles this family history to educate visitors about a darker chapter of Australia’s past.

Bardi man Terry Hunter on the beach at Cygnet Bay Pearl Farm, where he is the fourth generation of his family to live and work.

“For Bardi (land) and Jawi (island) people like myself, goowarn, or pearl shell, is a sacred link between land and sea. It’s one of Australia’s earliest forms of currency. I’m a fourth-generation pearler and Aboriginal Australian; my great-great-grandfather, Harry Hunter, was a notorious blackbirder who seized Indigenous people and forced them into slave labor. In the early pearling industry, through the 19th and into the early 20th century, blackbirders prized pregnant Aboriginal women as divers because there was a colonial myth that they had greater lung capacity so they could dive deeper and longer.

Today, I educate tourists about the pearling industry and my own family’s history, because I believe it’s time to acknowledge that slavery did happen in Australia.

The freshwater spring is one of our most important water sources. It has been naturally filtered through the beach sand, so it’s pure and full of natural electrolytes—our own ‘natural Gatorade.’

Our culture and food all come from watching this place closely. Each of our six seasons brings different winds, water, and animals. The wattle (Acacia) and the bauhinia (joomoo) trees serve as indicators, telling us exactly when to go fishing—when a species like mullet or trevally is at its best.

Timing matters with oysters too. In late June, they’ve just finished spawning, so they’re nice and plump. A traditional way of cooking them is to lay spinifex grass over the oysters and set it alight, so they pop open and smoke right there on the rocks.

Hunter cooks rock oysters the traditional way, heaping spinifex over them where they grow on the rocks and setting it alight. Once the flames die down, he prises the shells open with a pocket knife to reveal oysters that are warm and lightly smoked.

When you visit these shores, you’re moving through a living system of stories, tides, trees, seasons, and animals—each one telling us when to travel, what to hunt, what to leave alone, and how to respect this Country.”

A Jawi woman and founder of Oolin Sunday Island Cultural Tours, Rosanna Angus runs boat expeditions from Cygnet Bay across her people’s ancestral saltwater Country—work that saw her named Australian Tour Guide of the Year in 2023. Her itineraries retrace the story of the Sunday Island Mission, where her own family lived and led.

Jawi guide Rosanna Angus at Round Rock, near Ardyaloon (One Arm Point), with Jooloom Island behind her. As well as her regular boat tours, she leads women-only cultural journeys through Bardi and Jawi Country.

“We cruise past our community at One Arm Point, through billion-year-old Country where our Dreaming stories meet deep geological history, and into the Bardi Jawi Gaarra Marine Park, gazetted in 2025 after years of work between our people and government.

On Sunday Island, I tell the story of the old mission and my ancestors. My ancestor Igup was the first Chief of Sunday Island, and Kaori, from Boolnginy Island, was the last Chief of Sunday Island, handed the responsibility to look after the Jawi tribe. Our family name was originally Ungij, later changed to Angus by the missionaries. That history lives in old photos and stories I share on Country, where the mission stood. Our tribe is seven clan groups, five on the mainland and two on the islands, and I speak for Jawi Country through my ancestry and responsibility. We don’t have cave paintings here, so our history lives in our voices, our dances, our Ilma ceremonial objects, and the designs painted on our bodies—storytelling, for us, is governance, law, and identity.

Wild horses splash through rainwater on a red pindan track on the Dampier Peninsula. Beautiful as they are, these descendants of settlers’ horses are a declared pest in Western Australia, damaging Country and adding to the pressures on the peninsula’s endangered monsoon vine thickets.

Sharks hold an important place in our Sea Country and cultural stories; our totem shark is called Loolooloo. These connections, passed down through Dreaming stories, link our people directly to the ocean, our law, and our responsibilities to Sea Country. Sharks act as spiritual protectors for hunters and travelers navigating dangerous tides on traditional Biel Biel rafts, which is why we treat them with such deep respect.

Tourism keeps that culture strong and creates opportunities for our young people. I’ve been guiding since I was 16, inspired by my family, who’d always throw us in the deep end: ‘Come, you talk now.’ I’d rather collaborate than compete—sharing visitors with my brother, other guides, and local artists, so more of our community can care for this Country.”

Just a 10-minute drive from the skyscrapers of central Boorloo (Perth), Western Australia’s capital city, lies Kaarta Gar-up, or Kings Park, home to more than 3,000 species of Western Australian plants across its bushland and botanic garden. Steven Jacobs, a Whadjuk man and guide with In Culture Tours, explains why this land was so important to First Nations peoples, and how his community has fought to protect it.

Whadjuk Noongar guide Steven Jacobs at Kaarta Gar-up (Kings Park), with Boorloo (Perth) and the Derbarl Yerrigan (Swan River) behind him. At around 400 hectares, the park is larger than New York’s Central Park, and two-thirds of it is native bushland.

“Visitors from outside Australia are often surprised to find Indigenous culture here in the middle of the city. We’ve survived dispossession, the Stolen Generations, the massacres, and we’re still here, practicing and sharing our traditions with the world. In the Dreamtime, the Waugyl (Rainbow Serpent) moved across the earth, carving out rivers and mountains—not a god, just how our culture explains creation, without religion as it’s commonly understood.

Kaarta Gar-up isn’t just a park; it’s a cultural heart. Women came here to give birth, with everything they needed: reeds for baskets and mats, shelter, and fresh water from the Swan River. In our culture, women, the sun, and the river are the three main givers of life—we even use the same word, bilya, for river and umbilical cord. Women stayed here until the baby was ready to travel, then returned to the wider community.

The Pioneer Women’s Memorial at Kaarta Gar-up (Kings Park), a bronze of a mother and child unveiled in 1968 to honor Western Australia’s settler women. Long before it was built, this was a place where Whadjuk Noongar women came to give birth.

Our people lived off this river and land for thousands of years: fish, kangaroo, emu, plants, and bush medicines like a vapor rub made from peppermint tree, eucalyptus, beeswax, and balga resin. We were strong and healthy before European settlers arrived.

On Heirisson Island, just east of the park, stands a statue of Yagan, our greatest warrior, who fought British colonizers with a spear when they denied us access to the riverside. Eventually, they shot Yagan and beheaded him to claim a bounty; his head was later taken to England, exhibited in a museum, then buried in an unmarked grave.

Yagan’s head returned to Australia in the 1990s, and in 2010—177 years after his death—we finally laid it to rest, bringing deep spiritual healing to our people. It was about more than one man; it was about dignity, refusing to let our warriors remain curiosities in someone’s trophy cabinet overseas. They belong here, on their own land, with their own people.”

A Wardandi Bibbulmun woman known as the “Bush Tucker Queen,” Dale Tilbrook revives native food knowledge through Dale Tilbrook Experiences and Maalinup Aboriginal Gallery in the Swan Valley. With noncommunicable disease disproportionately affecting Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians, a legacy of systemic disadvantage, her work is about far more than flavor.

Wardandi Bibbulmun Elder Dale Tilbrook with her granddaughter Willow at Mandoon Estate, on Whadjuk Noongar Country in the Swan Valley. Here she and her brother Lyall run Maalinup (“place of the black swan”) Aboriginal Gallery, where visitors can browse works by Western Australian Aboriginal artists and taste bush foods such as quandong and finger limes.

“When people first smell cinnamon myrtle, they expect straight cinnamon, but what they’re really getting is the whole Christmas-spice family—the same compounds found in nutmeg, cloves, and mace. Lemon myrtle has the highest citral content of any plant in the world, which is why lemon myrtle tea is so powerfully antiseptic, antibacterial, and antioxidant, while anise myrtle helps with stomach cramps and chest congestion. Saltbush, meanwhile, thrives on marginal, salty land, and its leaves and seeds are rich in protein—everyday medicine built into what we ate and drank.

For tens of thousands of years there was no such thing as ‘bad food’ in our systems; everything we ate was nutrient-dense. Then came the settler-era ration system of white flour, sugar, salt, tea, jam, and tinned meat, and now we see very high rates of vitamin D deficiency, especially in remote Aboriginal communities. A lot of our work now is sitting with elders to pull old knowledge out of memory, and testing traditional foods for vitamin D and other micronutrients. We’re even finding that putting mushrooms in the sun for fifteen minutes before cooking can significantly boost their vitamin D content.

Finger limes are a native citrus that look almost like chilli peppers outside, but cut them open, and they release tiny, glistening pearls of juice—citrus caviar, packed with vitamin C and phytonutrients. Quandongs, sandalwood nuts, and desert limes are rich in everything from folate to B6. For us, these were simply the foods our Country gave us—but people call them ‘superfoods’ now, and they’re a blueprint for a more sustainable, nourishing future.”

For over 20 years, Juan Walker—a Kuku Yalanji man and founder of Walkabout Cultural Adventures—has guided visitors throughout his traditional Country, the Port Douglas Daintree region of Tropical North Queensland. He’s also a co-chair of the region’s First Nations Tourism Action Plan (FNTAP), working to put Indigenous tourism operators back in control of how their culture is shared.

Kuku Yalanji guide Juan Walker at one of his favorite swimming spots in Mossman Gorge, where the Mossman River tumbles over giant granite boulders at the southern end of the Daintree rainforest.

“FNTAP came about from a group of us—First Nations tourism operators from across the region—working with Tourism Tropical North Queensland to build a framework that properly recognizes that all tourism is on Aboriginal people’s Country. Coordinating a steering committee across a region this size, and making sure as many communities as possible were heard, was the hardest part of getting it off the ground.

For a long time, tourism products have been heavily restricted in terms of land access, even where Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people hold native title rights. Through this plan, we’re working with government agencies, hoping to ease those restrictions and create pathways for new Indigenous-owned businesses to develop and thrive. Historically, Indigenous tourism meant mass tourism—big numbers watching a quick dance or showcase, shaped by what non-Indigenous operators thought visitors wanted. Now we’re building fully Indigenous-owned operations with the freedom to teach culture and share our stories the way we want to.

Walker leads visitors across Kuyu Kuyu (Cooya Beach) at low tide in search of mud crab, just north of Port Douglas.

The places I take people are the same ones I grew up in, including swimming spots along Mossman Gorge where I went with elders, so everything feels natural and easy to take in. Hunting mud crab is part of that: we search for them through the mangroves and along the beaches, then cook them if time permits. The recipe is a family secret, but the key ingredients are coconut oil, garlic, chili, and brown vinegar.

This stretch of coast is the only place on Earth where two World Heritage areas meet: the Daintree Rainforest, around 180 million years old and one of the oldest tropical rainforests still standing, and the Great Barrier Reef just offshore. My people, the Eastern Kuku Yalanji, have lived along these coastal environments for thousands of years, and everything here is connected—land, sea, sky, and how we treat each other, governed by Lore, the law of the land. Through generations of observation, we’ve learned to live within it, not against it.

Dusk falls over Mossman Gorge. The valley sits beneath Manjal Dimbi, “the mountain holding back”: in Kuku Yalanji stories, its great rock face is Kubirri, who restrains the evil spirit Wurrumbu to protect the people below.

When people come out on Country with us, I want them to leave thinking differently—about this place, and their own home. Land and sea aren’t resources to use up; if we destroy where we live, we destroy our relationships too. Some of my strongest memories are being out here with elders, learning what the reef, rainforest, and waterfalls mean. That’s what drives me now: showing people the same love and respect for Country that was shown to me.”

#6703. The Shattered Bob Is Fall’s Most Wearable Short Haircut

Polished yet effortless, this is a look that can be easily tailored to every hair type.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The bob is undoubtedly the haircut of the year, and it shows no sign of losing momentum as summer gives way to cooler weather. While warmer days favored sharp edges and sculpted lines, this fall, the bob is taking on a softer, more undone shape, with a relaxed, less polished finish.

Enter the shattered bob: a tousled, textured take on the classic cut that captures the undone mood seen at London Fashion Week and on celebrities including Margot Robbie, Halle Berry, and Indira Varma. Natural texture is taking center stage, bringing movement and ease to a style once defined by sculptural precision.

The shattered bob is a softer, more relaxed take on the classic cut. It looks polished without feeling overly styled. “We’re looking at jaw-to-shoulder lengths, slightly broken edges, subtle graduation, and a heavier front. It should feel lived-in rather than perfectly placed, almost as though the haircut has naturally fallen into that shape,” say hairstylists Stephen Buller and Anita Rice.

Cut to fall softly and grow out seamlessly, it needs far less day-to-day styling while still looking considered. The style reflects a wider shift in beauty toward embracing hair’s natural texture and a style that feels authentic, luxurious, and easy to manage.

Movement is key to the shattered bob. Ask your stylist for soft, varied layers and lightly broken-up ends to add texture and soften the cut’s outline. It can work especially well with wavy or curly hair, as layers enhance its natural shape and movement.

Bring reference photos of people with a similar hair type to help guide the consultation. Your stylist can use them to tailor the cut to your natural texture and face shape.

Keeping products light is the best way to maintain the cut’s airy feel. Styling should be minimal, as the appeal of the look is in its effortlessness. “There’s still that polished fashion element, but it’s being roughed up. It feels more individual and ultimately more wearable,” add Buller and Rice.

For texture and separation without weighing the hair down, work a bit of a texturizing mousse or cream like Davines Dry Texturizer through the mid-lengths and ends.

Ultimately, the shattered bob should be about ease and hair that works alongside your lifestyle, showing that the most sophisticated hair often looks effortless.

#6702. How a Strip Club DJ Helped Xtube Kill the Porn Studio

For decades, anyone driving down the far-east stretch of one of Toronto’s main arteries would likely have caught a glimpse of a white Cadillac perched atop the entrance of a strip mall beckoning them to stop and step through a set of dark blue doors, behind which lay a world of male fantasy. So iconic was Caddy’s that when the strip club closed in 2017 the Toronto Sun sent out a reporter to mark the moment. In a story titled ‘Last Dance’, the paper somewhat melodramatically bewailed the end of an institution that had provided thousands upon thousands of Torontian men with an ‘escape from the drudgery of [ . . .] lives, wives and troubles’.

Judging by the long streak of one-star ratings on Caddy’s now inactive reviews page, its glory days were long gone by the time the classic car was taken down for good—and it wasn’t the only strip club to have suffered such a fate. By 2017 only twelve clubs were still operating out of the nearly fifty joints that had been dotted around Toronto at the turn of the century. Strip clubs have always been controversial, criticized for monetizing the objectification of women in a way many find too crude. Yet the stripper—at once desired and despised, exploited yet feared for her power to corrupt the good man—has not vanished. She permeates popular culture, from blockbusters and music videos to fitness crazes. Why, then, have strip clubs been shutting down? The reason was clear to Canadian stripper and activist Valerie Scott. “It’s called the internet,” she said in the report on Caddy’s closure; now, anyone seeking to escape the drudgery of reality had only to turn to their phone.

As fate would have it, Caddy’s made a cameo appearance in the story of how adult entertainment moved online. A little over a decade before the club played its last song it hired a man named Kurtis Potec, a former welder who’d just traded his tools for the DJ booth. “It wasn’t great; it wasn’t horrible,” Kurtis told me over a video call years later. “It was something to pay the bills.” Young and restless, he was a jack of all trades trying to find his way in life, but playing the tunes to which strippers danced and derobed turned out not to be Kurtis’s ultimate calling either. When he spotted a newspaper ad for a desk job at an online start-up not far from Caddy’s he figured he’d try his luck in the emerging virtual world.

“That was probably one of the most unique interviews of my life,” Kurtis told me with a chuckle. After a cursory skim of the twenty-something’s CV, the interviewer began to spout some “pretty vulgar, sexual-related terms” to check whether Kurtis was prepared for the world of online pornography. On the internet, there were no gatekeepers to control what people said, “so I guess they wanted to prepare me for the worst.”

He got the job. Kurtis’s new employer was Xtube, the first tube site targeted at gay men. The start-up’s first office was housed in a warehouse on the outskirts of the city, piled up to the ceiling and wall to wall with boxes, leaving only a two-foot-wide passage for Kurtis and his handful of co-workers to reach their desks. Inside the perilously stacked towers were countless pornographic DVDs awaiting digitization and to be uploaded online, along with merchandise like mouse pads and socks emblazoned with the company logo. Other than the three founders and the main financier—a Chinese man whom the others referred to as Mr X—the only other employee was a video encoder who at times appeared to live in the back room, where he worked and chain-smoked in solitude.

Kurtis, by contrast, was drawn into a far more public role. When one of the co-founders left, spooked by the threats that started rolling in from porn producers angry at finding their films on Xtube, Kurtis essentially picked up the day-to-day running of the site. Soon, he became the face of the company. Literally. “If you had any issues on the site, there was my ugly mug plastered in the corner,” he said. His associates didn’t use their real names, let alone their faces, and they had Kurtis—still technically a junior employee—front the company. “They were older and smarter than I was,” he told me, laughing.

By 2008, a year after Pornotube halted user uploads over fears of illegal content, business at Xtube was booming. Each month, it was pulling in hundreds of thousands of dollars from advertising. Advertisers were enthralled by this new medium, which allowed them to target their messages with unprecedented precision. Traditional media, including TV and magazines, had long promised access to certain demographics, but the internet offered the ability to drill deeper and glean details about people’s lives without asking a single question. Those being tracked hardly resisted. Many did not grasp the scale of the surveillance, while others were simply distracted by all the free stuff, like porn. Xtube’s users, Kurtis said, “really liked it.” But most of his days were spent fielding calls from within the industry, and their reaction was less enthusiastic. “People hated us.”

Around this time Kurtis started feeling depressed and began using drugs to cope with a job that, more and more, involved people shouting at him. “I got very used to hearing the words: I’m going to sue you.” But the threats were toothless. Free-speech laws governing the internet meant that user-generated platforms were, in essence, not legally responsible for what users uploaded.

All the studios could do was stand by and watch as their films were repeatedly stolen and re-uploaded by fans and, insiders complained, by tube sites themselves. It didn’t take long before their powerlessness began to attract investors’ attention. User-generated platforms seemed legally untouchable. And while there were plenty of platforms selling ad space, few received as many visits as the free porn sites. Kurtis was told to fend off callers claiming they wanted to buy Xtube. But one day in 2008 a man on the line refused to take no for an answer. He kept repeating: “Just give me a number.”

Kurtis walked into the back room, where one of the owners was sitting, and asked if there was any amount of money that would make it worth parting with Xtube. The slightly facetious reply was 35 million Canadian dollars. ‘I walked back, picked up the phone and said: “You’re not gonna like this,”’ Kurtis recalled. The man on the phone didn’t hesitate; he’d be there early next week to sort out the details.

In the months that followed a German in his early thirties would regularly occupy the carpet by Kurtis’s desk. Fabian Thylmann would stretch out on it to ease a back battered by his now frequent flights to Toronto. Fabian was a self-proclaimed nerd who as a teenager in the late nineties had developed one of the earliest pieces of software capable of tracking what internet users clicked on. Crucially, it allowed website owners to earn money when a link on their page redirected a visitor to make a purchase elsewhere. Hawking online advertising space had been a fairly unsurprising evolution of traditional marketing, but here was something that made it possible to monitor what people did next, and profit from it. The internet was turning into a game of digital chess, with money to be made by those who could anticipate, and manipulate, the whims of anyone who entered their domain.

Fabian’s first company had given him a rare glimpse into the back end of some early online businesses. Many were trying to sell porn, which was one of the first things people were willing to pay for on the internet. But these were small, makeshift operations, and few were making real money. In the early noughties, most of the people buying smutty DVDs or renting pay-per-views alone in hotel rooms hardly knew how to use the internet. Sure, they would eventually find their way to adult sites. But Fabian realized that a truly successful enterprise could do far more than tap into existing demand—it could bring pornography to people who had not even looked for it, through pop-ups, ads and search results, turning it from something you searched for into something that found you. Once porn became part of the internet’s background noise, those who’d never have dared to cross the threshold of a sex shop or an erotic cinema, or breach any of the other hurdles the curious had once faced, could now stumble upon porn with a single click.

The purpose of tube sites, like that of virtually every internet platform since, was not to replicate what existed in the physical world but to construct a new, disembodied mode of interaction built around visual stimuli—what we now call “content.” Their rise marked the start of a new era, when every step online began to be tracked. It was a turning point in the story of how data, harvested without people’s informed consent, became one of the world’s most valuable commodities, eventually proliferating to a point where it could be used to teach artificial intelligence to think and act like us. The tale of tube sites, then, is also the story of how the digital world came to be organized around priorities that do not necessarily align with those of the people who inhabit it.

The practice Fabian helped pioneer as a teenager is today known as affiliate marketing—put simply, the business of getting people to click on things. It’s how content creators make money when they offer their followers discounts on whatever must-have food supplement, skin cream or therapy app they claim to love. And the business of funneling people’s attention was first stress-tested in the porn industry. Long before influencers started peddling protein powder, porn sites were paying webmasters to drive clicks to their content, offering a cut for every paying visitor who came to their site through a tracked banner ad or link. It was the logic of the early thumbnail galleries, like the one built by the pale programmer who had filched sandwiches from Mario Salieri.

One of the key reasons why Amazon grew to become the place for online shopping was its early adoption of an affiliate programme which paid website owners a commission to direct people to products sold on the platform. Once people got accustomed to buying all their stuff on Amazon, the companies that actually made the stuff—anything from phone chargers to vacuum cleaners to cat litter—realized that if their products weren’t on the site, no one would buy them. Needless to say, affiliate marketing is still one of the main legs of Amazon’s business model, and its foundations were laid by people like Fabian, who understood that to make real money online you need to attract plenty of people and make sure they keep coming back. This is called “the network effect,” and it is one of the basic laws of the digital economy—the more people use your service, the more powerful you become.

As sites such as Xtube were attracting a critical mass of visitors, they could essentially dictate terms to studios that were now, in desperation, drawn into partnerships with the platforms. The tube site’s offer was to feature ten or fifteen minutes of footage and call it “advertising.” The only problem was that the average visit to a porn site ends—rather abruptly—after about nine minutes.

Still, as free content washed over the Web, studios started uploading their own clips to tube sites, hoping a few hundred or thousand viewers might click the affiliate link and pay for the full film. If they did, the revenue would be split 50:50 with the tube site. “We put a lot of studios out of business,” Kurtis said, “they couldn’t afford to get traffic from us.” Companies like Xtube quickly learned to steer what users clicked on next, and once they controlled enough traffic to funnel millions of potential customers towards paying sites or advertisers, they became powerful.

This dynamic has since spread beyond porn. Many news outlets now depend on posting their stories to Facebook, TikTok or X, hoping to lure readers back to their own sites, where some might eventually pay for their journalism. Few do. Like porn, news has become something most of us expect to get for free. The number of independent newspapers has collapsed, many swallowed by conglomerates that rely on scale to profit from advertising and, increasingly, from affiliate links.

Fabian’s ambitions were clear from the beginning. Xtube was offering more than a quick buck. It was a stepping stone in the making of an empire. He wanted to “basically take over the adult industry,” Kurtis said. As the traditional studios buckled under the tube-site business model, many went up for sale, which meant that their huge libraries of content could be bought on the cheap. For a site like Xtube, buying studios and their subscription platforms made perfect sense. It gained access to more content, and could funnel its huge traffic towards paid sites it now controlled. If people paid for porn, the company profited; if they preferred the free stuff, it profited too.

It was a business model that thrived on relentless expansion, and Fabian had his sights set on a much bigger rival. In nearby Montreal, another group of young men were running a site that would become to pornography what McDonald’s is to the burger: Pornhub. To simplify, it was founded in 2007 by three Concordia University students—Matt Keezer, Steph Manos and Sam Youssef—whose company, Mansef, was already running several porn businesses, including the still influential production studio Brazzers (a slang take on “brothers”). Publicly, Youssef posed as a concerned studio owner and railed against tube sites on the industry forum GoFuckYourself.com: “They will not steal it and get away with it. Their days are counted!” What few in the industry realized was that Pornhub was run by the same group.

In a 2023 interview about his most recent venture Youssef said that he and his co-founders made the decision to sell Pornhub to Fabian in 2010 for roughly $140 million because he “didn’t feel comfortable at all with what the company had become.” He sounded almost surprised to have found himself in the sex industry, despite having made his money from sites such as JuggFuckers and RacksAndBlacks.

When I tried to contact them all in 2020, Youssef declined to talk to me about those early years, saying he was never really “much involved” with the business he had founded. Keezer likewise responded: “To be honest with you, I never had any involvement in the ‘industry.’ I just made Pornhub in 2007 with a couple of friends and sold it [ . . .] and that was about it.” I had no response from Manos. This detachment was typical of the internet entrepreneurs who profited from unleashing pornography. Many preferred to remain anonymous, even as the industry’s most important workers literally have to bare all. In a move that reflected the trolling culture of the nerds who were taking over porn, Fabian—the new king of smut—renamed his empire Manwin.

#6701. These Long-Lasting Tubing Mascaras Survive Sweat, Tears, and Long Days

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

I’ve always been particular about mascara. I need a formula that lengthens my lashes to the heavens, won’t flake or smudge, and stays locked in place from morning to night. After years of testing and reviewing mascaras as a beauty editor, I’ve found that there is only one type of formula that manages to do it all: tubing mascaras.

The best tubing mascaras are in a league of their own. Instead of simply coating lashes with pigment, they wrap each individual lash in tiny, water-resistant polymers that form a flexible “tube” around the hair. The result? A mascara that won’t smear, flake, or run throughout the day, yet slides off effortlessly with warm water when it’s time to take it off.

It almost sounds too good to be true, right? The best tubing mascaras do feel like magic—team Cosmo would know. We’ve tried every tubing mascara out there, and somehow we narrowed our favorites down to this list of seven foolproof (and smudge-proof) formulas, below.

Why we love it: Ask any beauty editor or makeup artist what their favorite tubing mascara is, and most will mention this magic formula. “Liquid Lash Extensions is the tried-and-true, the pioneer of tubing mascaras,” says professional makeup artist Brittany Whitfield. “It’s my absolute favorite for length.” This takes natural lashes to new heights and won’t smudge—even in high heat—yet it still easily washes off at the end of the day. Plus, the formula comes in eight hues, ranging from black to ivy green for plenty of makeup experimentation.

One Cosmo editor says: “I’m a bit of a mascara snob, and I always find myself coming back to this formula. This is completely flake and smudge-free and keeps my lashes looking full and long until I wash my makeup off at the end of the night. It’s a top three mascara of all time in my book.” — MARY HONKUS, CONTRIBUTING BEAUTY EDITOR

Why we love it: For those who want more natural-looking fringe that still appears fresh after 12+ hours, Merit’s clean formula is ultra-reliable. This imparts a soft black tint and ever so slightly lengthens lashes to achieve the no-makeup makeup look in just a few swipes.

One Cosmo editor says: “Clean Volume is the perfect name for this surprisingly un-clumpy volumizing mascara. The formula coats every lash, making my eyelashes look thicker and more fanned out, but it doesn't give them a spidery or clumped together look at all. The wand really helps separate every lash, and it even helps hold a curl for quite a few hours.”—BETH GILLETTE, BEAUTY EDITOR

Why we love it: Don’t let the mini wand on this mascara deceive you—this mascara packs a lot of punch into just a few swipes, and helps you get into all the crevices of your eye to coat every last lash. And it easily comes off with a cleansing balm or some micellar water, without pulling out any of your precious hairs.

One Cosmo editor says: “This tiny mascara should be considered sorcery first, a beauty product second. #6698. Lisa Is Officially A Showgirl

Tomorrow, Lisa Manoban—the singer, Blackpink member, and The White Lotus star—makes Las Vegas history. For six nights, she’s bringing “Viva La Lisa” to the City of Sin, becoming the first-ever K-Pop star to have a Las Vegas residency. The tickets sold out in an impressive 10-minutes flat, and cities were added due to voracious demand.

Today, though, the Thai multi-hyphenate is still in prep mode. Skin prep, to be specific. “My biggest goal is to keep my skin healthy and glowing,” she tells Vogue in an exclusive interview. “Especially with all the traveling and makeup I wear for performances.” Earlier this year, Lisa was announced as the global ambassador for Shiseido’s Ultimune collection. The sleek red bottles befit the Vegas bathroom of any great showgirl. She calls the Power Infusing Serum “an essential step in my routine,” because it helps her meet her healthy skin goals.

Las Vegas has a storied history of showgirls—the glamour! the sequins! the physicality!—and Lisa, who is known for her love of sparkles, beauty, and all things flamboyant (she introduced the world to the fuzzy smiling gremlin that is Labubu, after all) is prepared to live up to the hype. She also hopes that she’ll find a little spare time to do some adventuring around the city. “There are so many amazing performances in Vegas right now. If I have time, I’d love to watch something I haven’t seen already.”

During that off-duty time, don’t expect her to be in full La-La-Lisa glam. “On show days, I pay a little more attention to hydration since I’ll be wearing makeup for hours,” she says. “On mydays off, I like to keep everything as simple as possible.” And while a sold-out residency may mean some late nights, there’s always one beauty rule that’s a non-negotiable when it comes to protecting her poker face: “My mom always reminded me to take care of my skin, even when I was tired,” she says. That’s stayed with me, so no matter how late I get home, the first thing I always do is remove my makeup before bed.”

Finally, after months of preparation, the time has come for her to step onto the stage. “Before going on stage, I like to stretch, relax for a second, and then say a little prayer,” she says. Luck be a lady—and her name is Lisa.

Where some other awards-bestowing committees have been notoriously late in giving great directors their flowers, GQ refuses to waste time. He is also, now, about to embark on another massive adventure, though this time in our solar system: Villeneuve will be directing the next James Bond film.

To celebrate the man behind the camera, GQ will host a conversation between Villeneuve and Zach Baron, host of One More Question, followed by a special screening of Dune: Part Two to get everyone ready for the third-and-final installment. This all happens tonight at the newly opened, architecturally stunning Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles.

Come back next Tuesday to read Baron’s profile of Denis Villeneuve, part of GQ’s Men of the Year issue.

#6694. 8 Best Mascara for Older Women Lift and Volumize Lashes of Any Age

Time changes everything, including our eyelashes. “As we mature, our lashes can naturally become finer, shorter, and less full, so I’m always looking for the best mascaras for older women to bring back that beautiful definition and volume,” says Melinda Melrose, Dolce & Gabbana Beauty’s global makeup expert.

According to Melrose, those best-in-class mascara formulas add definition, lift, and an elegant flutter to any makeup look, and they’re easy to incorporate into an everyday makeup routine. Her technique? “Start right at the root, gently twist the wand as you sweep upward,” she says. “Really focus on lifting those lashes rather than just coating them with product. The goal is to open up the eyes, not weigh them down.”

J. Brandon Correa, YSL Beauty’s national makeup artist, finds that the right mascara can enhance the appearance of each individual lash. “Definition can be just as impactful as volume, especially when working with mature eyes,” he says. “Ultimately, creating beautiful lashes isn’t always about adding more; it’s about understanding how to enhance what is naturally there.”

A light-handed approach is especially flattering on mature women. “Going too bold can weigh the eyes down and make them appear smaller,” celebrity makeup artist Tonya Riner notes. “Use feather-light strokes to avoid applying too much product at once. It is always easier to add than take away.” She also advises moving the wand in one direction, working from the base of the lashes to the tips in clean, precise strokes. “This helps the product distribute evenly,” she explains. “Avoid back-and-forth motions, which increase the likelihood of clumps.”

Since sagging skin can make the lashes harder to reach, it also pays to know a few hacks for making application a breeze. To wit: “I take the makeup wand and slightly bend it so it’s more at a 45-degree angle,” says Chicago-based hair and makeup artist Kate Johnson. “This allows you to hold the mascara wand at a more comfortable angle while getting closer to the lash line.” (Bonus: Johnson says there’s no need to straighten the wand out before inserting it back in the tube—it will automatically adjust.) Meanwhile, Riner likes using a wand with “small, tooth-like bristles” for easy, ultra-precise application.

Of course, it doesn’t hurt to find a formula that curls, lifts, lengthens, and separates. Ahead, see the mascaras pro makeup artists and Vogue editors recommend for lashes worth batting at any age.

For older women, Paul recommends mascaras that offer both volume and length, since lashes can lose density and become shorter as the hair-growth cycle slows down. “Curling mascaras are also great, because they provide lift to the lashes that really helps to open up the eyes,” he says. This is key for older women: Over time, biological factors such as the loss of orbital fat and weakening eyelid muscles can make the eyes appear smaller. As for Bryan, “I tend to prefer lightweight or tubing mascaras,” he says. “I find these types of mascaras don’t put a lot of stress on the eyelashes and still provide ample support and lift.”

What to Look For in a Mascara for Older Women

For older clients, “I like to look for mascaras that contain nutrient-rich ingredients to help condition and treat the lashes over time,” Bryan says. “I personally tend to steer away from waterproof mascaras to avoid them possibly flaking into the eyes.”

According to Paul, customers should also consider wand size. “Smaller, deep-set, and hooded eyes do best with smaller brushes that can reach every lash, even into the corners of the eye, without creating a mess on the eyelids,” he says. “Larger eyes work well with mascaras that have big, fluffy wands.”

For sparse lashes, Paul recommends choosing volumizing mascaras that will build the lash to create the illusion of fullness. “It’s also great to pair a mascara with a primer like Diorshow Maximizer 4D that not only builds up the lash before mascara but also nourishes and strengthens the lashes as you wear it,” he says.

Wand shape comes into play here, too, and Bryan recommends amping up sparse lashes with a mascara that has a smaller brush that’s easy to control. “That way, you can build up volume and length without clumping the sparse hairs together with a larger brush,” he says. Thinning lashes should also consider formulas that feature conditioning ingredients like botanical oils, butters, and waxes which help limit breakage.

What color mascara is best for older women?

According to Paul, the best way to choose a mascara color is to consider one’s overall color intensity. “Brunettes pair well with black mascara, blondes and redheads with brown mascara, and navy works well with grey hair,” he says. He adds that navy mascaras are also ideal for tired eyes on anyone. “They enhance the whites of the eyes to make them appear well-rested and bright,” he says.

Should older women put mascara on the bottom lashes?

Paul says choosing where to place your mascara depends on a few factors. “If you are aiming for a lifted appearance, then only wear mascara on the upper lashes,” he says. “However, if looking more lifted isn’t a concern, then you can also apply mascara to lower lashes.” A hack to get the best of both worlds: apply brown or navy mascara on the lower lashes to add subtle definition. “Then, apply black mascara on the upper lashes to really define and open the eyes,” Paul suggests.

The key to removing mascara is to avoid tugging at the eyes. “Eye makeup removal is one of the most overlooked steps in a beauty routine, yet it is absolutely critical to maintaining healthy skin and lashes,” pro makeup artist Lauren D’Amelio Ventre previously said. “After nearly two decades in the beauty industry, working with everyone from brides to celebrities, I’ve seen how improper removal can age the eye area prematurely or lead to irritation, and how the right products can completely transform the skin’s resilience.”

You want to choose something with slip to seamlessly remove water-resistant or long-wearing eyeshadow, eyeliner, or concealer. Start with a micellar water or cleansing oil, then cleanse with your face wash and rinse with warm water.

We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

To do this, we paired our own personal tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine which we would recommend to you.

#6693. If You Didn’t Already Think CrossFit Was a Cult, This Book Will Convince You

CrossFit could easily hold the distinction of being the most popular—and certainly the most universally recognized—fitness movement ever. At its peak, the company, founded in 2000, boasted over 15,000 affiliate gyms, or “boxes,” in more than 150 countries and was enlisting nearly 50,000 coaches each year. Somewhere along the line, to many people (including my mom), the word CrossFit became synonymous for working out.

But you may have noticed that people don’t talk as much about CrossFit nowadays as they used to. Following an assorted variety of allegations against its mercurial founder Greg Glassman in 2020, and the tragic and seemingly avoidable death of an athlete at the 2024 CrossFit Games, the company has been gradually losing its chalky grip on popular culture.

But the storytelling around CrossFit’s rise and fall is anything but done and dusted, as I learned while reading Calum Marsh’s new book, The Glass Box—a fascinating, staggeringly detailed account of not only CrossFit’s rocket-propelled rise and spectacular flame-out, as told by insider sources including Glassman himself, but a trove of previously unshared anecdotes that make it hard to put down.

A few days after the book’s late-October release, I spoke to Marsh about airing CrossFit’s dirtiest laundry, how the cultishness of CrossFit has spread to other fitness crazes, and why an old-fashioned barbell snatch is the ultimate kryptonite for the modern performative male.

Calum Marsh: The first 50 people I spoke to were basically warning me off the subject, telling me that it was going to be an uphill battle and that if the people that I was writing about were unhappy with how I wrote about them, they would criticize me or attempt to defame me. They have a long history, which I've chronicled in the book, of creating campaigns of bad will towards their critics. They are really experienced at mobilizing the internet and mobilizing social media in order to discredit people that they consider critics or, as I sometimes frame it in the book, heretics.

But, on the other hand, I knew that I was going to be approaching this from a journalistically rigorous perspective, and that it was going to be an account of what actually happened, from the people who were involved. It wasn't going to be a book about my opinion or my personal take on CrossFit. So I felt quite secure that the things I was writing in the book were the best possible representation of the truth.

There's been a lot of focus on some of the more, shall we say, sordid details. There was an article in the New York Post that basically pulled all that out and made the book seem like it was some scandalous hit piece. That's not the book I tried to write, and it's not the book I think I wrote. The book I wrote is a very fair, even-handed assessment of a man and the business that he created. It includes true stories about his behavior that may not be the most flattering, and it includes, I think, testament to the brilliance of what he created and all of the great things that he did.

It's been amusing to see the reception somewhat split among some hardcore CrossFitters. They're upset because they think it's a takedown of Greg Glassman that's biased against him. And then other critics think that I'm way too generous to him, or way too flattering. Someone said I was too affectionate towards him. It's funny to me that two different people can read it and have polar opposite views. But hopefully that means that it's just objective.

It’s something that is always mentioned in relation to CrossFit. There’s actually another book that came out while I was writing my book, called The Cult of CrossFit by Katie Rose Hejtmanek. It's an academic study of the history and sociology of cults, and how CrossFit is a cult by definition. I thought that was really illuminating. There are a lot of similarities that go beyond all the joking, and there are a lot of things about the cult-like nature of CrossFit that have made it intoxicating for some people, and maybe painful in other ways as well.

The thing that struck me was how a lot of people, especially earlier CrossFit enthusiasts or devotees, talked to me about the difficulty they had leaving CrossFit. Greg has said many times, and will still say, that they weren't a cult because you could leave at any time. And I always found that to be a fairly unconvincing argument, because many cults say the same thing. A lot of CrossFitters had this experience where they felt like they had really close friends—sometimes even family members or partners—who essentially excommunicated them—cut them off, iced them out, however you want to phrase it—after they either left CrossFit or spoke out against CrossFit. That, to me, is the strongest cult-like parallel.

It really wasn't. I had heard from people that Glassman was generous, and so I knew stories about him spending lavishly on dinners, for example. But it all seemed pretty much within the realm of normal spending for someone who's massively wealthy. It wasn't until I started speaking to people who were more familiar with CrossFit’s finances when I started to learn about the degree to which the spending was out of control. The amount of money they spent relative to what they earned is the most shocking thing to me, because it's not like they were spending that much money while wildly out-earning it. They were almost spending more than they were making. And they were not slowing their spending when the earning slowed. That, to me, as a business reporter, is very, very interesting, because you start to wonder how they let that happen. Was no one there to say, ‘Hey, we need to pump the brakes a little bit?’ As it turned out, there really wasn't.

A lot of people had this reckoning in 2020 after [Glassman’s George Floyd tweet] and some of the accusations that came out about Glassman then. A lot of gyms deaffiliated from CrossFit, and Greg, of course, stepped down and sold the company. I personally know many people who had a kind of personal reckoning with their level of comfort in supporting the company. But I think that was, at least in some cases, answered by Greg's departure.

Others went through this process of divorcing themselves from the CrossFit identity as a brand, but continuing to practice CrossFit as a methodology. There are thousands of gyms all over the world that are CrossFit gyms in all but name. They probably call themselves cross-training or functional fitness now, but if you go in, they still have a Rogue rig, they still have wall balls, they still do snatches—everything you'd expect to see if you walked into a CrossFit gym. The people there are still CrossFitters at heart. They've still given themselves over to the transformative power of the methodology that Greg Glassman invented. But they are no longer endorsing or supporting the brand or the company at large.

I would be willing to bet that if you walked into any CrossFit gym in North America and asked them what the difference is between when Glassman was in charge and when corporate private equity took charge, they wouldn’t know that even happened. The average person, who just goes to CrossFit to get fit and doesn't follow the CrossFit news and isn't obsessed with CrossFit Games, would not have any idea. And this is partly a consequence of the fact that the affiliate model is so loose.

I first started going to a box in 2018. I was doing personal training with someone at what I didn't realize was even a CrossFit box. I was doing that personal training for probably about a year before I realized I was doing CrossFit, and then I started doing classes in 2019.

I do! In fact, I coached a CrossFit class earlier this morning.

Yeah. Well, they don't allow you to call it a certification with the one I have. They're very clear about that language. But I do have my CrossFit Level 1 certificate. I did the course and passed the test.

I think that part of it is just the nature of fandom. If you become enthusiastic about something, you want to identify as an enthusiast, and that means wearing the T-shirt. I went to a Bob Dylan concert on the weekend. I bought a Bob Dylan hat. It's just part of the experience of being a fan of something. I think Hyrox is super interesting, because it does have a lot of cult-like similarities with CrossFit. But the really toxic side—the side that's a bit more nefarious, that involves really giving your life over to it—I haven't seen with Hyrox, at least yet. I feel like there's something missing at the center, possibly the guru figure that Greg Glassman was for CrossFit. Hyrox doesn't really have that. So maybe that missing ingredient has stopped it from being as intense. But, on the whole, I think it's just this level of fandom that is baked into everything in culture now.

There's a journalist named Hannah Singleton, who writes about fitness a lot. She recently wrote a piece about how athleticism is the new flex for people, and I think that’s sort of the direction we're moving in. For example, Hyrox. It's in the same vein as running a marathon or doing an ultra race, where it's an achievement that you can brandish. You can put it on your LinkedIn. You can say that you've done this and that. Maybe it's on your resume. You're almost putting up points on your scoreboard. And I think that we're probably going to find either more events along those lines, where it's something that you can be proud of because it's so difficult, or a system in which you can have an overall fitness score. I think people really want to show that they put in the work. They want to impress people with how fit they are. In the same way that people who are into running are obsessively posting about their marathon time or their 10K time, and those milestones are universally understood in running—everyone knows how impressive it is to run a sub-10-minute 5K or a sub-three-hour marathon—the fitness equivalent of that, I think, is still coming.

This is one of the things I find interesting in light of CrossFit—and I know that some people are going to think this is not true—but I really do think CrossFit, or let’s say functional fitness, is an antidote to this whole performative thing. It's so hard that it's humbling. You can’t really show up and pretend you did it. You cannot performatively do barbell snatches. If you see someone on social media snatching heavy, it's because they've worked at it for hundreds, if not thousands, of hours, and because they're really strong, really mobile, and really fit. And I say this as someone who both has a copy of Infinite Jest on my bookshelf and wears Satisfy.

You can ‘perform’ your sport of choice by posting about it, but things like snatches or ring muscle ups are so physically demanding that it kind of cuts through that bullshit. And I think that we're probably going to increasingly value things that we know on-site are authentic, because there's an authenticity built into it. There's no shortcut there. And that authenticity will become more and more valuable.

#6690. Hanifa Is Relaunching After an 8-Month Hiatus

Hanifa is back. A little over eight months after founder Anifa Mvuemba paused operations for her label, which had been in business for 15 years, it’s relaunching with a new collection and updated business model.

The collection features the colorful party clothes the brand is known for, like a red evening gown with a bright blue feathered brooch and a blue liquid organza dress (a 2022 revival bound to become the season’s made-to-order showstopper). There are also more practical pieces, like Hanifa’s take on the track pant (barrel-legged with a silk stripe) and bomber jacket. The Harper dress, a green and black-dotted hit from last year, is now available in a deep blue.

Mvuemba hopes the new Hanifa feels true to the brand’s original ethos, just a little more mature: the designer was 21 when she started the brand in 2011, and now that she’s about to turn 36, her style and taste has evolved, she says, alongside her customers’. Mvuemba spent months reworking the brand’s fabrications, cuts and patterns, especially for knitwear, its biggest category. She went through dozens of iterations to find the right cashmere blend, for example, that will hold its shape and have cashmere’s soft handfeel, while keeping the brand in the price range its customers have come to expect.

The brand worked to improve its fabric quality without compromising on price.

The relaunch will be a test in regaining consumer trust. Things began to unwind last December, when purchases made during her brand’s annual Hanifa Friday sale in November failed to ship, thanks to production delays and supply chain issues. For some customers, they said months went by without any communication — or delivery — from the brand. Disgruntled customers took to social media to complain, not just about delayed orders (all of which Hanifa said it was eventually able to fulfill, or issued refunds for), but about the brand’s general direction, which they believed went downhill. In a statement posted online in March, Mvuemba apologized, and announced the brand would go on hiatus.

“Mentally, I wasn’t prepared to continue,” Mvuemba says. “I wasn’t in the right headspace. And in order for me to be the best version of myself, the best leader, mother, wife, I could be to my family, my team, my business — I needed that mental clarity to just take a step back, rest, recalibrate, to get a clear view on what we needed to do for the business as a whole. I needed a break,” Mvuemba says. “I’m just not the type of founder or person that performs for the optics. It was extremely hard to do, but it was necessary, because in this space, it’s not something that we see often. But it’s something that we as founders need to be able to do.”

Hanifa’s new collection comes after the brand paused orders in March.

In the end, Mvuemba only took about two weeks off from work, she says. She found a therapist and spent time with her baby, who was born in December and whose maternity care was interrupted by crisis management in the fallout. Then, she turned her attention to Hanifa 2.0.

“I love this business so much. I love this brand so much. I had to get back,” she says. “We uprooted everything. We looked at our communications, our branding, our sizing, our website. Now, everything — our processes, our manufacturers — has shifted, and it’s nice to have had this time to sit through everything, go back, revise, go back, revise, and then say, ‘OK, we’re ready.’”

Now the brand is ready to relaunch, Hanifa is returning to market on different terms.

Mvuemba is eyeing outerwear as an expansion opportunity for her collection.

The biggest change to Hanifa’s operations is switching to a fully ready-to-ship model, versus a past pre-order model. With no pre-order period, where the brand could produce only a committed number of SKUs, the company has fronted the entire new collection (which Mvuemba says is “expensive but necessary”) and plans to use real-time performance data to determine production cadence and inventory investments. Having inventory overhead also shortens lead times for purchases to be fulfilled, and gives the brand space to ship items by sea rather than air, which cuts costs.

“We thought it was really important to come out the door swinging,” Mvuemba says. “People want their things when they want their things.” It’s also invested in new customer service and logistics partners, with brand plans to build data analysis into its production cycle to ensure that it’s responding quicker to what’s selling. Mvuemba hired a brand strategist, an art director and a PR firm to help steer the comeback story. The brand has always been bootstrapped, but she says she’s open to outside funding if the right partner comes along. She’s also open to the right retail partners, but that right now, the direct-to-consumer model is the best fit thanks to production and shipping timing.

Her focus above all, she says, is her customer. Mvuemba comes back time and again to the importance of data, and how much she wants to spend the rollout of this collection listening to feedback. She hopes that the brand’s core customer — the company has a legion of longtime loyalists who were sad to see it go — returns, and that the brand can grow its reach. By category, she’s excited about expanding the brand’s shoes and outerwear, both of which are steps in building a more complete ready-to-wear label, which is her main goal for next year. Scaling, Mvuemba says, will come at the right pace.

“I used to say I want it to be as big as LVMH. And with this year, I just had so much time to reflect and I’m OK with the pace that we’re going,” she says. “I just want to have a globally recognized brand that a lot of women can identify with and that we can continue to create these beautiful, amazing pieces. I’m so excited to show them this new era of the brand. We’re sharper, we’re clearer, we understand who our girl is, who our customer is, and I’m excited to give them more.”
