#6655. Frico'ed Brussels Sprouts

A slick of oil and a sprinkling of salt are the only adornments brussels sprouts need to shine. But put a crispy Parmesan skirt on them and suddenly the humble veggie becomes the belle of the ball. This recipe does just that. By roasting the brussels sprouts snuggled into a blanket of grated Parmesan cheese, the cheese melts into a crispy, frico-like sheet that clings onto the sprouts, surrounding them in a lace-like halo. It’s a dramatic side dish, but one that makes a serious statement. If roasted correctly, and the stars align in your favor, you can peel off the entire sheet in one swift swoop, presenting it as the culinary masterpiece it is. Fans of fun, this is for you.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a baking sheet with a nonstick baking mat or a sheet of parchment paper generously coated with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a medium bowl to combine. Scatter 4 oz. store-bought grated Parmesan (pre-grated works better here than grating from a block) in an even layer over baking sheet, leaving a ½" border around edges. Arrange brussels sprouts, cut side down, in a single layer on top, spacing evenly to fill baking sheet. Bake until brussels sprouts are tender and browned and cheese is deep golden, 20–28 minutes. (If the cheese in the very center is browned, it’s done.) Let cool at least 5 minutes, then break into pieces to serve. (Or place another parchment-lined baking sheet upside down on top; holding together, swiftly turn over, peel away mat, and present cheese side up.)

#6654. The 6 Winter Coat Trends Defining the Season

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

From sculptural tailoring to vintage-inspired faux fur, these are the styles to know

A great winter outfit deserves an equally great coat, especially when it’s an essential layer for the next several months. Beyond the practical need for warmth, outerwear often sets the tone for an entire look as the first layer you see. A sharply tailored wool coat can make jeans and a sweater feel more polished, while an oversize silhouette or rich texture brings dimension and new proportions to otherwise clean-lined looks.

For fall/winter 2026, designers are rethinking classic outerwear through distinctive silhouettes, textures, and details. At Ferragamo, Tory Burch, and Fendi, precise tailoring took a dressier turn, with slim silhouettes, tuxedo-inspired designs, and satin lapels bringing eveningwear polish to wool coats. Meanwhile, Ralph Lauren, Mugler, and Burberry embraced leather for a sleeker city-ready take on winter dressing. Faux fur took on a distinctly vintage feel at Stella McCartney, Bottega Veneta, and Khaite, while plush collars added texture to everything from elegant overcoats to more everyday designs.

Whether you’re looking to invest in a forever piece or simply want something fresher than the coat you’ve worn for the past few winters, these six trends offer plenty of inspiration.

Faux fur is taking a distinctly retro turn this winter, with plush textures and elegant silhouettes reminiscent of vintage finds. Stella McCartney’s floor-grazing belted coat and Bottega Veneta’s voluminous fur both recall the glamour of the ’30s and ’40s, while Khaite’s shaggy cream jacket has more of a ’70s feel, particularly when dressed down with jeans. Of course, we love a faux-fur coat as the finishing touch to a dressy outfit, but there’s something even chicer about pairing one with everyday denim and boots.

Arma Verena Reversible Shearling and Leather Coat

A black coat is hardly a groundbreaking winter choice, but the fall/winter 2026 runways offered plenty of reasons for the wardrobe classic to be in focus. Designers showcased timeless silhouettes with subtle updates to keep things more interesting. Think sharp, menswear-inspired tailoring with a more formal finish at Celine or oversize cuts and dramatic lapels at Michael Kors. Tod’s introduced a different kind of drama with a sleek, draped cape design, proving that black is never boring.

Polo Ralph Lauren Wool and Silk Crepe Tuxedo Duster Coat

Favorite Daughter Metropolitan Wool and Cashmere Blend Coat

The Row Ciara Wool-Cashmere Belted Wrap Coat

There’s a certain refinement to a beautifully tailored coat, especially when the details borrow from formalwear. Think precise cuts, elongated silhouettes, and tuxedo-inspired touches that feel polished enough for an evening out. There’s a more dressed-up sensibility to these classic designs—as seen at Ferragamo, Tory Burch, and Fendi—from the precise fit to the smallest finishing details. This attention to detail brings a beautiful sense of sophistication to workwear and when paired with simple everyday separates.

Gap x Victoria Beckham Wool-Blend Chesterfield Coat

Mackage Elodie-R Double-Breasted Wool-Blend Coat

When a puffer or classic wool coat feels too predictable, a leather coat offers a much bolder alternative. Ralph Lauren, Mugler, and Burberry all embraced waist-defining silhouettes, from classic double-breasted trenches to softer robe-like shapes. In dramatic maxi lengths, the effect is especially sleek, with just the right amount of edge, bringing a bit of bite to winter dressing.

Nili Lotan Arsene Leather Double-Breasted Trench Coat

The Frankie Shop Edra Shearling-Trimmed Wrap Coat

Gray was ubiquitous on runways from New York to Paris, appearing in everything from textured tweed to draped wool and sharply tailored shapes. Whether you prefer deep charcoal or soft dove, it’s an easy neutral to wear in tonal layers or to balance bright colors and prints.

Banana Republic Herringbone Wool-Blend Top Coat

Marant Etoile Pilda Herringbone Double-Breasted Coat

’S Max Mara Scarf-Detail Virgin-Wool Wrap Coat

Faux fur was all over the fall/winter 2026 runways, even in smaller doses like plush collars. If you know that feeling of a sharp chill hitting your neck when the rest of you is bundled up, these collars offer the warmth you need in an ultra-elegant way. On everything from sporty puffers and classic toggle-front wool coats, as seen at Louis Vuitton, to the patterned and pretty pastel trims at Chanel and Gabriela Hearst, it’s a detail that’s as practical as it is beautiful.

#6653. Netflix Is Stepping Onto the Ice With an Icebreaker Adaptation—Here’s Everything We Know

Hockey romances aren’t just dominating bookshelves anymore; they’ve become television’s newest obsession.

Following the breakout success of recent sports romances like Heated Rivalry and Off Campus, Netflix is officially joining the trend with a series adaptation of Hannah Grace’s bestselling novel Icebreaker. The BookTok sensation, which helped introduce a new generation of readers to the hockey romance genre, is headed to the streamer as a college-set drama centered on a figure skater and a hockey player whose ambitions—and attraction—begin to collide.

Here’s everything we know about Icebreaker so far.

Yes. Netflix announced on June 15 that it has greenlit a television adaptation of Hannah Grace’s novel Icebreaker.

The project was unveiled during the Banff World Media Festival by Jinny Howe, Netflix’s head of scripted series for the U.S. and Canada.

In a statement, Howe said, “Netflix has a long history of turning beloved romance novels into massive global hits. We know our members can’t get enough of these stories, which makes Icebreaker the perfect next chapter for us.”

She added, “By supercharging the hockey sports romance genre, Icebreaker has ignited a passionate fandom and helped redefine the landscape of contemporary romance. We are thrilled to partner with Jade Bartlett, Amanda Lasher, and the team at Unwell Productions to bring this irresistible love story to life.”

The series follows Anastasia Allen, a competitive figure skater focused on reaching the Olympics, and Nate Hawkins, a star hockey player with dreams of going professional.

Their paths cross when an accident forces their teams to share the same rink, creating tension both on and off the ice.

Netflix’s official synopsis reads, “She’s the transfer gunning for Olympic gold. He’s the campus star chasing the NHL. But when an accident forces their teams to share one rink, Anastasia Allen and Nate Hawkins collide—and discipline gives way to obsession, because the only thing more dangerous than wanting to win is wanting each other.”

The adaptation will be set in the same college sports world that readers first fell in love with in Grace’s novel, blending romance, competition, and the pressures of elite athletics.

Yes. The show is based on Grace’s 2022 novel of the same name.

As the first book in Grace’s Maple Hills series, the novel’s popularity eventually expanded into a larger franchise, with follow-up books Wildfire and Daydream taking place in the same university setting.

Amanda Lasher has signed on as showrunner, writer, and executive producer. Her previous television credits include Gossip Girl (2008–2012), Riverdale (2017–2018), and The Bold Type (2018–2019).

Jade Bartlett developed the adaptation and wrote the pilot. She will also write and executive produce the series alongside Lasher. Bartlett’s previous projects include Road House, Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, and Miller’s Girl.

“I love this genre, and it’s been a joy working with Jade, the team at Unwell, and Netflix to bring Hannah Grace’s beloved Icebreaker novel to the screen,” Lasher said in a statement.

Bartlett added, “It’s been such a joy to play in Hannah Grace’s world of Icebreaker, a story filled with ambitious, talented, and undeniably sexy characters. But the real special sauce is that, above all, they are good, deeply compassionate people.”

The series will be executive produced by Unwell Productions, with Alex Cooper, Matt Kaplan, and Mina Lefevre serving as executive producers.

On September 28, Deadline revealed the show’s two leads. Daisy Kelley and Connor Simos will star as Anastasia “Stassie” Allen and Nate Hawkins, respectively.

On September 29, Gabriel Tierney (Rivals, Enola Holmes 2), Auliʻi Cravalho (Moana), Peter Berry, Chaneil Kular (Sex Education), Devin Craig (Sex Lives of College Girls), and Aidan Shaw (We Were Liars, Heated Rivalry) were also announced as cast members on the show. According to Deadline, “Tierney will play Aaron; Cravalho will portray Lola; Berry is Robbie; Kular will play JJ; Craig will portray Henry; and Shaw is Russ.”

On November 11, Netflix announced that Paul Wesley (The Vampire Diaries) will also be joining the cast of Icebreaker. He’ll star as Coach Neil Faulkner in the series.

The series does not currently have a release date, but the show is currently in production in Vancouver, Canada.

#6652. Jamie Campbell Bower Is the Rising Style Star You Need to Know

When it comes to Hollywood’s red carpets, the menswear assortment is—more often than not—very safe. Snoozy, even. Sure, classic suits and tuxedos will always have a place at a splashy movie premiere, but whatever happened to fun? No one’s fun anymore!

That being said, there are a few actors who are taking a more eccentric and unexpected approach to their fashion choices. Take Alexander Skarsgard, and his freaky shoes. Or, more recently, there’s Jamie Campbell Bower, who has been bringing a unique fashion energy to his press tour for The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power this month. (The star recently joined season three of the hit Prime Video series.)

You may know Bower for his music, or for portraying the villainous Vecna on Stranger Things, but we are fast associating him with an impeccable sense of style. Throughout his press tour this month, he and his stylist Nathan Henry have been infusing traditional tailoring looks with cool, off-kilter accessories—like brooches and headpieces!—that make the outfits feel a whole lot more fresh and modern.

Last night in London, for one, Bower emerged wearing a black cape coat from Matières Fécales—the avant-garde Parisian label that is fast becoming a celebrity favorite. Punctuating his sleek outerwear? There was a bejeweled crown headpiece, oversized eyeball and flower brooches, and even a spider-like jewelry piece that fit like a glove. Talk about fun!

Wearing pieces by Wooyoungmi, John Richmond and Adelina Bernard.

Some of his other recent Lord of the Rings looks have been more subdued—but equally as slick and contemporary. For the New York premiere, there was a perfectly-slouchy black pinstriped suit with layered silver necklaces; For the Mexico City screening, he chose a black suit with a burgundy velvet lapel, and a crisp white shirt with a high collar and oversized lapels. These slight exaggerations of silhouette imbued his looks with a little personality: They’re not so formal or standard; rather, they have a little zest to them.

Given he is also a professional musical artist by day, Bower’s rock-and-roll sensibility could play a big part in why his red carpet style feels so noteworthy: He simply has that innate, effortless way of dressing that so many musicians seem to nail. (Think: Mick Jagger, Prince, Bowie.) And we need this energy from a whole lot more men in Hollywood. . . Life is short: Take a risk!

#6651. 'Wild Horse Nine' Should Win an Oscar for Its Signet Rings

Wild Horse Nine is a Western. Sort of. Yes, Martin McDonagh’s new film is set on Easter Island (known locally as Rapa Nui) in the Pacific Ocean. And yes, this is the 1970s, with John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell playing CIA operatives who take a break from plotting a coup in Chile to tour the stone moai heads.

But there are also—as the title suggests—a lot of wild horses about, plus a cameo from Tom Waits in a shack in Colorado’s Monument Valley and a hell of a lot of Western accessories. Rockwell’s turquoise belt buckle and cowboy hat almost had me wanting to jump back in time and become a paid-up member of the American deep state. And the big signet rings with chunky stones everyone’s wearing? Look, if you really need me to fictionally assassinate JFK and frame Lee Harvey Oswald for it, I’ll step up.

Costume designer Eimer Ní Mhaoldomhnaigh, who worked with McDonagh on The Banshees of Inisherin, had fun outfitting everyone in colorful shirts and flared trousers. “I really liked the way men dressed in the ’70s,” she says. “There was almost a dandyish quality to them.” But it’s the accessories that really makes the characters. “Anytime you’re doing a fitting [for] a male actor,” she explains, “you’re putting on the shirt and the trousers and they’re like, ‘Mmm, okay.’ Then you put on that belt, you give him a Cuban heel and a cowboy hat and a ring, suddenly they start to stand differently. They get the whole swagger. A costume is never finished until you have all those details.”

This is a film with a lot of those details. Rockwell’s cowboy hat, for example, was custom-made by the London milliner Sophie Lamb, who's worked on films like Phantom Thread. His belt buckle is in the traditional Navajo style of the American West: sterling silver with turquoise inlay, which Mhaoldomhnaigh says she “probably got it on Etsy.” That said, she does a lot of IRL trawling on London’s Portobello Road, too. “I really wanted Sam to wear a chain, but when we put it on with the whole outfit, it felt like overkill—like we were decorating a Christmas tree. You have all those things and then you have to pull back a little bit.”

There’s other great gear in the vein of brash, peacocking men of action. “It’s a very American look,” says Mhaoldomhnaigh. Steve Buscemi, who plays the CIA’s South American boss, is in Coblens glasses with gradated lenses, and a ’70s watch from Rotary. Rockwell has a chunky gold watch from Pierre Jacquard. Malkovich, whose character is still stuck in his ’60s glory days, has this whole pork-pie hat thing happening.

But what really gets me going is the rings. Pretty much everyone—including Waits, who plays Malkovich’s hippie brother—has got these chunky rings on, and of a kind we don’t necessarily associate with gray-suitness of the American establishment today. It’s more dandyish, as Mhaoldomhnaigh puts it: “I was a child in the ’70s,” she says. “I always remember older men wearing those type of rings. My dad had one.”

She was on the lookout for designs which matched her memories, both vintage and new—Malkovich’s ring, which is gold with a black onyx stone, was “actually bought in Liberty,” she says, referring to the famous British department store.

“Martin’s films are always a little bit heightened,” the costume designer says. “That’s part of the fun of it, being able to create these slightly heightened characters.” And dressing up those characters means you can have fun, as McDonagh does, in mocking their big egos. Even so, I’m being deadly serious when I say I’d ransack Mhaoldomhnaigh’s props box any time.

#6650. Schmaltzy Chicken and Stuffing Skillet

While you might think of instant stuffing as a once-a-year darling that makes an annual appearance like Punxsutawney Phil, this recipe is a case study of why this product should be put to use throughout the year. (Boxes of the dried mix can be found near the breadcrumbs any month.) Here, it’s called into action to prop up skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs in a bed of savory stuffing that’s bolstered by aromatics and sweet-tart dried cranberries. Starting with a cold pan ensures even rendering of the chicken fat and crispy skin. The lot gets baked together, allowing the savory drippings from the chicken to soak into the stuffing. Serve with a side of cranberry sauce, a fresh salad, or all by itself for a one-pan dinner that recalls Thanksgiving any night of the week.

More delicious skillet dinners this way: Chicken Thighs With Spiced Couscous and Carrots; Ruffled Mushroom Pot Pie; and One-Skillet Chicken Pot Pie.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Season 2 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (about 4 medium) on both sides with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Pour 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil into a cold large stainless-steel skillet and swirl to coat bottom of pan. Arrange chicken, skin side down, in pan and place over medium-high heat. Cook undisturbed, rotating pan around on burner often to promote even browning, until skin is browned and chicken releases easily from pan, 7–10 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet or large plate and arrange skin side up.

Combine 1 large onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan and cook over medium-high heat, stirring often, until onion is softened and just starting to turn golden, 8–12 minutes. Add one 6-oz. box instant stuffing mix, ½ cup unsweetened dried cranberries, and 1¼ cups water, then finely grate in zest from 1 lemon and set lemon aside. Mix until stuffing is hydrated. Remove pan from heat and push stuffing to sides to create wells for chicken to rest in. Nestle thighs, skin side up, into stuffing. Transfer pan to oven and bake until chicken is cooked through and top of stuffing is golden brown and crisp, 45–55 minutes.

Top chicken and stuffing with more dried cranberries and reserved celery leaves. Cut reserved lemon into wedges and serve alongside for squeezing over.

#6649. How Olivia Munn Takes the Edge Off

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The actress shares the beauty and self-care essentials she swears by, including a $75 volumizing cream

Welcome to Take the Edge Off, a series that breaks down the beauty and self-care routines of influencers, CEOs, experts, and celebrities. Find out how they unwind and decompress, and take a closer look at the holy-grail essentials they’re raving about.

Life can throw unexpected surprises—good and bad—your way, and many lean on wellness practices to stay grounded in chaos. Olivia Munn knows this firsthand. The actress was diagnosed with early-stage Luminal B breast cancer in early 2023, thanks to what she refers to as the “life-saving” risk assessment test with renowned obstetric and gynecologic surgeon Thaïs Aliabadi at the helm. With a toddler and fresh off a double mastectomy, Munn turned to meditation to find her footing through it all.

“I always associated meditation with having to quiet your mind, and I couldn’t imagine how anyone actually did that, but over time, I’ve come to understand that it isn’t about stopping the noise in your head; it’s about learning not to be carried away by it,” Munn tells Bazaar. “I don’t feel the need to chase every thought or immediately make sense of everything. I can just let things settle without feeling responsible for figuring them all out.”

That same strength and balance are exactly what fashion label Anne Klein wanted to embody when the brand enlisted Munn as ambassador for its fall/winter 2026 collection and to continue spreading her message.

Ahead, we caught up with Munn about what else keeps her present during times of stress, from the manifestation candle she loves to light to words she lives by.

“The future you is depending on the you today to do the right thing.” This means the me today depended on the me three years ago to go to the doctor, get the MRI, and face cancer head-on. I was depending on the me last week, month, or year to start working out more, learn that new language, or organize my closet. When I think about how fast time goes by, and how tomorrow, next month, and next year come in the blink of an eye, it motivates me to take the first step toward whatever I want to do.

A couple of months ago, I began using prescription-strength azelaic acid and tretinoin. I start with azelaic acid, then tretinoin, and finish with the Volume Cream by Adipeau, my holy-grail moisturizer.

My favorite cream right now is Adipeau’s Volume Cream. I’ve reached the point in my life where my hands and neck are showing signs of being crepey. A friend told me about this cream and promised me that if I used it every day for a month, I’d see a difference, and she was right. The science behind it is incredible, so incredible that I often worry about whether the company is doing well because I need them to stay in business forever.

My makeup goal has always been no-makeup makeup. But it is incredibly difficult to master, especially on yourself. My hat’s off to all the influencers who do it so beautifully; I see you and wish I were you.

Shige brand cuticle oil. The amazing manicurist Shige [Taylor] created her own nail line, beginning with an incredible cuticle oil made in Japan. [My] nail bed has never looked or felt so hydrated.

Yes, I light candles from Aloha Elixir. They’re made in Hawaii and are really special, intentional candles.

When I start getting anxiety, which I often do, or have difficulty falling asleep, I do this breathing technique that activates the parasympathetic nervous system, which controls our “fight-or-flight” response: Breathe in through your nose for four beats, hold for seven, breathe out through your nose for eight beats. It calms my system down, and the anxiety goes away, or I drift off to sleep. I do it three to six times, sometimes a little more. But it always works for me.

#6646. Get Huge’s Director on How Looksmaxxing Is a ‘Trap’ for Men

Chasing physical perfection is a hobby now. This year, the community of men obsessed with climbing the ranks of society via square jawlines and hunter eyes, became a subject of widespread fascination. Once a term known in niche internet forums in the early 2010s, the concept of “looksmaxxing” has gone mainstream. These days, even the casual scrollers among us have probably heard of techniques like bonesmashing and mewing.

But beyond a few self-appointed figureheads of the movement, the question of who is buying into these extreme self-improvement measures has loomed large. In Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death documentarian Stacey Lee gives viewers a deeper look into the lives of some of the looksmaxxing community’s more controversial figures. The three-part Hulu docuseries, out now, follows bodybuilding and biohacking influencer Dr. Tony Huge (whose real name is Anthony Hughes), controversial fitness personality, Connor Murphy, and a handful of other men.

Set largely in Thailand, the series tells the story of how these influencers decamped abroad and continued to post near daily videos of their body modification techniques. Lee also confronts the disturbing pattern of deaths among Huge’s inner circle, some of which have gone unsolved. Ultimately the series raises larger questions about the cultural, gender-driven motivations to push the limits of their bodies. GQ spoke with Lee about her nearly two-year immersion into a small corner of this community, the blurred lines between online persona and reality, and what it all reveals about a generation of young men who are seemingly searching for identity, connection, and purpose through increasingly unhealthy outlets.

These internet influencers create so much content, and there's a performance of masculinity that takes place within it. The topic is incredibly polarizing, but also very nuanced. We wanted to capture this world in a way that was more dimensional than what YouTube feeds allow, puncturing the veneer of performance to show who these people are beyond their online personas. I want audiences to see a more multifaceted view of this world and decide for themselves how they feel about these characters based on what they're seeing.

Looksmaxxing wasn't even a term when we started this project [in 2024]. We initially entered the bodybuilding, biohacking, and masculinity influencer community, which was still very fringe at the time. Tony had started making content nearly a decade ago, using shock value and radical transparency to build his brand. He was willing to do things on camera that others wouldn't, challenging social taboos. Ten years later, we're seeing a new generation of influencers who grew up watching Tony, [biohacking YouTuber Leo and Longevity], and Connor and are now using similar methods. But the algorithm has shifted the goalposts significantly since 2016, pushing the content into a much more extreme and nihilistic space.

I wouldn't necessarily say he was the godfather of looksmaxxing, but he was certainly influential in the biohacking and bodybuilding space. Connor Murphy was probably more directly connected to the origins of looksmaxxing, and Clavicular has referenced him as an inspiration. Tony was part of that same world, but represented a different generation.

Tony was a larger-than-life figure, but it was also a broader cultural moment. Around 2016, we were seeing the first Trump presidency, the post-Me Too movement, and the rise of Red Pill philosophy. There were several figures galvanizing these ideas, and Tony was among them.

I think what you're also referring to is this idea of legacy, right? He created something he believed was his unique gift to the world, but there's a sense that the next generation doesn't recognize him or understand his influence. That disconnect seems to drive some of his pursuit of the next big thing, which, in this instance, is looksmaxxing.

Look, Tony is incredibly charismatic and easygoing. Honestly, filming with him was a really respectful process. I think at times it was really discombobulating because he's always smiling in these videos, and he's presenting as this happy-go-lucky kind of guy, but then you're stopped in your tracks because he's doing and saying things that run against that.

The only other reference I'm thinking of is Andrew Tate, who presents in this very sinister way and has a darkness to him that's front and center. Tony doesn't present that way. For us, it was important to show that and to dimensionalize him. In his eyes, he didn't care if he was a hero or a villain. He just wanted to get his story out there. My approach was that I wanted to humanize him, but it wasn't about excusing what was happening.

It's important in this day and age to approach controversial subjects with an element of humanity while still maintaining journalistic independence. In this world, the boundaries are really slippery because people are performing so much. You really have to have your guard up about what's real and what's not. I don't think it's my job to tell audiences what to think of Tony. It's my job to provide a fuller understanding of who he is and allow them to make up their own minds. Discernment was something that was really important for us to communicate: What you see is not always what you get.

You see it in episodes one and two. [Editor's note: Tony lives with his wife and a group of other women he refers to as his girlfriends.] There's a very specific mentality rooted in Red Pill philosophy, where the role of a man is to control these women and provide for them, but also to assert himself. He's the leader, and they must follow. I think one of the things Tony is always battling is that he presents in such a nice way and isn't aggressive like [his friend and fellow biohacking influencer] Leo was, but there's still this desire to control the women. The women are very strong, opinionated women.

From conversations with Tony during the making of this documentary, I know a lot of the women didn't realize they were coming into a harem. They thought they were his one and only true love, and then they've entered this environment and suddenly they're in competition with one another.

That competition is part of the dynamic of how the harem works. The way Tony puts it is that if they're in competition with one another, they try harder to vie for his attention, love, and affection. That's an incredibly complicated way of pitting women against each other, and somewhat dehumanizing.

What I want to be really careful of is that these aren't a bunch of outrageous, crazy people doing crazy things from the start. It actually begins in a real human place, a place all of us can relate to. I want to be the best version of myself. Yeah, of course I do. That's very relatable.

What happens within this is that some of the needs, in Elon [Muscular, one of Tony Huge’s mentees and a content creator]'s case, a sense of belonging, a father figure, all of those kinds of things that he's craving, aren't solved by taking one pill. These are really deep societal issues that are complex and need to be approached with a multidimensional complexity.

Therein lies a lot of the challenges with this world, because the extreme and the attention keep pushing those goalposts further. You get a bigger jawline, a bigger penis, bigger muscles, and you're still not feeling happy. I think it creates this kind of trap that some men can get stuck within, because the original solution was never going to solve that problem to begin with.

Honestly, it was really important for me to make this. A lot of my prior work has centered on women and diverse perspectives, and it's such an honor and privilege to do that kind of work. But I also recognize I was existing in a bit of an echo chamber, so doing this project took me well outside my comfort zone.

I use this example with kids: When they're scared at night, you shine a light in the room. You look under the bed, you shine a light into it, and it makes the thing that's inside your head less scary. There was a little bit of that in making this documentary, of really looking at it and understanding it, witnessing how people come in, why they stay, and why they also can't leave, and using those things as what I need to teach my son. I need to teach him discernment. I need to teach him the difference between a YouTube influencer who's performing and one who's actually giving genuine, real tips.

In this day and age, where clipping culture and soundbites matter, there's no room for context. We're in a post-truth era, and no one's taking the time to provide context, human dimension, or other perspectives. I want my son to understand how the internet and influencer culture work so he can make his own decisions with more critical thought than what's often taught in the public space.

Yeah, of course. I never wanted to make something that was just another echo chamber. I want this documentary to reach people deep in the heart of the masculinity influencer space. I want them to see it. Everyone's going to have a different reaction, but most importantly, people are talking, and that's what I care about. I need the conversation, the depth of the conversation. That's what this is designed to have.

It's interesting because that question has come up a few times. There does appear to be a turning of the tides. Even within Tony's own universe, his sense of relevancy has shifted. He went from being the most masculine man he could be to wearing eyeliner. It's all become a lot more fluid and therefore a lot more interesting.

I think there's a time we're living through where the power structures that have existed for the last decade are starting to break down. People aren't feeling connected to them anymore, or they certainly aren't serving their needs.

I hope we're at a time of reckoning and change, where people are recognizing that this isn't working. There's so much more awareness about the issues men are facing, and there are specific influencers who are the opposite kind, who are speaking about this stuff more. There are some incredible voices in this space starting to counter the other perspectives out there.

#6645. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6644. Is Astrology Right or Left?

Like many aspects in American life, astrology is experiencing a political reckoning

In 1988, a former aide to President Reagan alleged that Nancy Reagan relied heavily on the astrologer Joan Quigley to guide key moments in her husband’s presidency. The Reagans denied that characterization, but the image of an easily swayed Nancy Reagan using some irrational force to push through Reagan’s policy decisions entered general pop culture, fueled in part by the misogyny of the political press toward most women in politics, left or right, in the 1980s.

The story of Joan Quigley and Nancy Reagan is part of a larger history of people turning to the stars to help explain, and potentially influence, political events. This is an impulse that doesn’t belong to any particular political ideology. But in current pop culture, astrology is often used as shorthand for liberal or leftist worldviews. Leading up to the 2024 U.S. presidential election, some online astrologers confidently celebrated a potential Harris win. Their despair over the actual outcome was reported in numerous outlets. It seemed to confirm the stereotype of who follows astrology: millennials who are deeply disturbed by the current state of the world.

Today, astrology, like weight lifting, holistic medicine, and organic farming, has become less a hobby and more a political signifier. So many practices that used to be read as lifestyle choices—tracking your macros, for instance, or taking up ceramics—have, in our hyperpolarized culture, become stand-ins for a person’s political leanings. But what’s curious about astrology is that it reads as liberal-coded to those outside the field and potentially conservative to those inside it.

In a 2022 piece titled “Astrology and the Search for Meaning” in The American Conservative, Bradford Tuckfield attributed the rise in astrology to the fact that cultural discourse had “damage[d] or destroy[ed] the …positive myths that used to animate people,” adding, “The patriotic idea of America as a great nation has been undermined by many efforts for decades, the most notable recent example being the ‘1619 Project.’ ” For conservatives like Tuckfield, astrology is an attempt to fill a vacuum left in the American psyche. The absence of religion and the demand that citizens grapple with uncomfortable historic truths supposedly left young people ideologically lost. “The myth of social justice seems to have absorbed much of the energy” of young people, Tuckfield claimed. And astrology is just like that “myth.” For conservatives, then, astrology is just one of many cultural challenges to a homogeneous culture built on the myth of the hero. Astrology, in their reading, leads to challenges to the status quo, which is, by definition, the antithesis of conservatism.

But that’s how outsiders view the field. Astrology also has its own organizational bodies that strive to define the discipline and often are administered by older, more politically and culturally conservative practitioners. But those groups’ influence over astrology has waned as it has become more accessible through the internet. Once-esoteric knowledge is now widely distilled through TikToks and live streams, and this has led to a political divide for many astrologers.

“To be able to study astrology historically has been a very privileged thing to do. And so it’s been dominated by white folks,” explains the astrologer Chani Nicholas. Nicholas is a popular astrologer who trained with those unaffiliated with traditional astrology organizations. “There’s very explicit reasons why I’ve not invested a tremendous amount of time in general astrology communities, even though I am massively indebted to the community and I have a deep appreciation for it,” she says.

Nicholas’s brand of astrology makes explicit connections between planetary transits and real-world political events. She directly cites progressive and leftist political goals in the context of astrology. Nicholas traces the political divide in astrology to post-pandemic America and links it to the same divide seen in alternative health spaces and yoga practices, where many practitioners became enthralled with MAGA and MAHA politics while others did not.

Before the pandemic, organized astrology was dominated by “a group of white people that are mostly able-bodied, mostly heterosexual, mostly cisgendered, that have never had to confront their own racism, sexism, homophobia, transphobia,” she notes. “In the pandemic, a lot of millennials started taking classes with a lot of establishment teachers, and a lot of the racism started to come out.… Millennials were like, ‘I’m not going to sit here and have you say that. You can’t say that.’ And then the more establishment teachers were like, ‘Why are you coming for me?’ ”

This tension between a more conservative old guard in astrology and a younger group of practitioners came to a head this summer when Stephen Forrest, an older practitioner of astrology, appeared on the Lila Astrology podcast. In the episode, he spoke about a satirical character he had once employed to make fun of racism, using the N-word in doing so. Forrest also brought up white-supremacist beliefs he had previously held on the inferiority of Black people’s intelligence; claimed to be related to Nathan Forrester, the founder of the KKK; and repeated the debunked myth that the KKK originally formed as a charity organization and not a terrorist one.

In response, younger astrology adherents asked that Forrester be removed as a speaker from an upcoming conference. Other older practitioners who were more deeply invested in astrology organizations cautioned against “cancellation.” Chani Nicholas, who was scheduled to appear at a conference that was also planning to host Forrester, pulled out of her appearance.

“Astrology attracts all these different types of people. It’s fascinating, but it doesn’t mean that because you’re interested in the human condition that you’re actually interested in interrogating your own biases and your own way of enacting violence on behalf of the system,” Nicholas says.

Astrology organizations, like many institutions currently, are caught between a younger generation, which is asking an older one to abide by the values of fairness and universal acceptance many purport, and older generations that are refusing to see the contradictions and biases in many of their organizations’ stances.

“There was no shared reality about where we had been working,” says Nicholas. “This younger generation of people that were really trying to understand identity and politics and location and power and privilege started to make this robust astrology community [of their own] and really push back against a lot of stuff that had just been existing unchecked for decades.”

Samuel F. Reynolds is an African-American astrologer who, for more than 35 years, has chosen to work within astrological organizations. He originally came to astrology as a skeptic. One of the biases he pushes against is the tendency to ground all interpretations in Western culture. “When Uranus went into Libra, an older Western astrologer might say to you, ‘Oh yeah, that led to a time where there was an acceleration of divorces and where people started to gain more power related to marriage,’” Reynolds explains. “When they say things like that, I’m like, ‘Oh, okay, did that happen in Africa? And did that happen in India? Was that true in most of Asia?’ And the data actually is no, it didn’t happen during that same time frame.… It does bring up a philosophical question of what are we talking about and what are we looking at? Because the framework by which we talk about humanity is not quite as vast as astrologers like to believe when they talk about it. That’s the truth of it. You’re talking about the people who are like you or in some way who are adjacent to you.”

He remembers astrology conferences 20 years ago where “every other talk, someone would bring up the charts of the Beatles, Princess Di.” Astrology is an art of interpretation, which rests on the practitioner’s frame of reference. The limited references at conferences spoke to “the insularity in general of white people,” Reynolds says. He does note, though, that at a conference recently, he saw someone comparing the chart of Toni Morrison with Agatha Christie. “Why? I’m not exactly sure,” he jokes.

All of this conflict is happening in the wider context of big cultural and political shifts and the crumbling of any sort of authority or governing bodies. In extreme instability, the desire to understand why everything is changing makes astrology even more attractive. And astrology offers a lens for many to understand themselves. You may not be able to name why you have anxiety or why you tend to have chaotic romantic relationships or why you have trouble forming deep community bonds, but your planetary signature (and those of your friends and lovers) can provide you with something that looks like an answer.

But Nicholas cautions against giving too much sway to the question of transcendence and self-interrogation that astrology can sometimes provide. “I really want to talk about how we can build power and be effective now,” she says. “I don’t want to be out in outer space. I actually really want to be on earth.”

#6643. Korean Hair Vinegar Is the Secret to Glossy, Glass-Like Hair

If we’re being honest, shiny glass hair takes quite a bit of work. There’s the salon gloss every few weeks, the shine serum before you leave the house, and the professional blowout that never looks quite as glamorous the next morning. So when a two-minute shower step started promising the same mirror-like finish, it was bound to take off.

Enter Korean hair vinegar, which has been all over TikTok lately, with videos of dull, frizzy hair turning smooth and shiny after a single wash. It might sound like something you’d put on a salad, but the idea has deep roots. “In Korea, vinegar has always been both food and medicine,” says Ellie Byun, OMD, a doctor of Korean medicine and licensed acupuncturist.

Still, vinegar isn’t exactly the first thing you’d reach for to fix your hair, and plenty of viral trends don’t exactly live up to the hype. So does this one? Below, experts break down what hair vinegar actually does, who should try it and who should skip it, plus a few of our favorite formulas.

At its simplest, Korean hair vinegar is an acidic rinse that finishes the job your shampoo starts. “Shampoo lifts and opens the hair and scalp, and hair vinegar is the finishing step that settles everything back down,” says Dr. Byun. “Hair vinegar is to shampoo what toner is to cleanser.”

The idea isn’t new, but the format is. “The old kitchen version meant guessing at the ratio and hoping for the best, but the downside is that it could leave hair feeling stiff,” says Michelle Lee, chief marketing officer of K-Beauty World and former editor-in-chief of Allure. Dr. Byun points out that homemade rinses are also hard to get right. “The difference is that the strength changes every time you mix it, and if it’s too strong, it can irritate the scalp,” she says. “Korean formulas adjust the pH and add botanicals like green tea or mint, so you get the benefits without the guesswork.”

So why is it suddenly everywhere? “I think it’s kind of a classic case of an old idea getting a modern update,” says Lee. Most of the credit goes to glass hair. “Glass hair is about a smooth, light-reflecting cuticle, and vinegar is one of the simplest ways to get there,” she says. For many Korean women, it’s been part of the routine for years.

It mostly comes down to pH. “A healthy scalp has a pH of about 5.5, and the hair fiber is about 3.67, so both are naturally acidic,” says Byun. “Alkaline products increase the negative charge on the hair surface, which creates static, friction, tangling, and frizz. An acidic rinse reverses that.” Once the cuticle lies flat, hair reflects more light, which is where the shine comes from. “On the hair, a well-formulated acidic rinse can help reduce static and friction, leaving strands smoother, less frizzy, and easier to detangle,” adds Kristin Lim, founder of Base-K.

It can also help with dullness caused by buildup. “Vinegar also helps break down product and mineral buildup, which is often why hair looks dull in the first place,” says Lee. “It’s a gentle reset more than a miracle.” It’s not a substitute for a good shampoo, though. “Acidity alone does not guarantee effective buildup removal,” says Joe Cho, Team Lead of Media Relations at Medicube.

Lee says Korean hair vinegar works especially well for “people with hard water, since mineral buildup makes hair look flat and feel rough,” along with anyone who uses a lot of dry shampoo or styling products. Color-treated hair can benefit, too, since a smoother cuticle makes color look shinier. Byun also recommends it for finer textures. “It works well for fine hair that falls flat easily and scalps that get oily quickly,” she says.

The most obvious benefit is shine, and you’ll usually see it after one wash. “A mildly acidic wash or treatment helps the cuticle lie flatter, so hair looks shinier and feels smoother,” says Lee. If you color your hair, there’s another bonus. “It’s also wonderful for color-treated hair, because a smoother cuticle makes color look more vibrant,” says Byun. For oily scalps, it can even leave things feeling fresher between washes.

Acid isn’t gentle on every scalp. “If your scalp is very dry or sensitive, skip it or use a very mild formula,” says Byun. “Skip it if you have eczema, psoriasis, or any broken skin. If you have dandruff or seborrheic dermatitis, start with a medicated shampoo.” Ingredients matter, too. “Even a formulated hair vinegar can irritate some people, depending on its acidity, fragrance and other ingredients,” says Lim. And if your hair is badly damaged, keep your expectations in check. “While acidic products may temporarily improve smoothness, they cannot reverse structural damage,” says Cho.

Order matters here. Use it after shampoo and before conditioner, and there’s a reason for that timing. “Right after shampooing, your hair and scalp are at their highest pH, so that’s when an acidic rinse works best,” says Byun. Work it through damp hair and onto the scalp if the product says it’s safe there, then follow her method: “Leave it on for one to three minutes, rinse with lukewarm or cool water, then apply a light conditioner, mainly on the ends.” Some formulas are leave-in, so always check the label first. If you’d rather make your own, Byun’s ratio is a good place to start. “Dilute one to two tablespoons of apple cider vinegar in about two cups of water and start mild,” she says.

Less is more when it comes to how often you should use this type of product. “Start with once or twice a week. If your scalp is oily or your water is hard, you can use it a bit more. If your hair is dry or fine, use it less,” says Dr. Byun. Your hair will let you know when you’ve overdone it. “If your hair starts to feel squeaky or straw-like, that’s the signal to scale back,” says Lee. “I’ve found that less often usually gives better results than more.”

“For color-treated hair, choose a rinse specifically labeled color-safe. ‘Hair vinegar’ alone doesn’t guarantee compatibility,” says Lim. After a fresh color appointment or a keratin treatment, give it some time. “Just wait a few days after coloring or a keratin treatment, and check with your stylist,” says Dr. Byun. If you wear extensions, Lee recommends caution: “With extensions, keep the products away from tapes, bonds, and glued areas, since some can loosen with certain ingredients.”

So will your hair end up smelling like vinegar after use? Yes, but not for long. “And acetic acid, the compound behind the vinegar smell, is volatile, so most of it evaporates as you rinse and your hair dries,” says Dr. Byun. Most formulas also add fruit or floral scents to cover it. “It’s a tangy note in the shower and then it’s gone,” says Lee.

Look for a formula that lists its pH and tells you how to use it. “A brand that shares its pH and provides clear usage instructions is a good sign,” says Lim. Lee is even firmer about that: “If a brand won’t say anything about pH, I’d skip it.” Soothing ingredients like green tea, centella, panthenol and glycerin are good signs, while heavy fragrance and drying alcohols are worth avoiding if your scalp is sensitive. “‘Natural’ doesn’t automatically mean gentler,” says Lim. And skip anything that promises too much. “Be wary of claims like ‘treats hair loss’ or ‘regrows hair.’ There’s no evidence that vinegar does that,” says Dr. Byun. Shop our favorite formulas, below.

We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

#6642. What James Gunn’s Firing Means For the Future of DC Studios

For some reason, I foolishly believed they’d get it right this time. James Gunn’s Superman, which formally launched the DC cinematic universe he’s been masterminding alongside Peter Safran, was a refreshing take on a somewhat impenetrable character. I had some reservations about the rest of Gunn’s proposed slate—like following that movie with a Supergirl adventure, which proved to be every bit the misfire I imagined it would be—but bringing a contemporary Clark Kent to the screen was no small accomplishment. Gunn’s tone and his sensibility, I thought, might finally make way for the silver-screen Justice League adventure we deserved.

A silly hope, as proven by Monday’s big news: Gunn and Safran are out, in the wake of the WB-Paramount-Skydance unholy merger. Yet another auteur’s DC regime has been clipped before it could even find its footing. After the shock of the announcement wore off, my mind immediately went to that James Franco meme, the one where he’s about to be hanged. First time?

20 years ago, the idea that superhero C-listers like Iron Man and Thor would be at the top of the film adaptation pyramid while the stars of the Justice League toiled in a constant cycle of developmental destroy-and-rebuild would have been laughable. That’s part of what makes Kevin Feige’s MCU so impressive, of course: not just the scale and scope of his interconnected series of films, but doing it with a bunch of guys who were never all that popular in the larger superhero firmament. But as that regime rose, DC’s fortunes seesawed—with the Christopher Nolan Bat-trilogy as a beautiful outlier—and its fans have had to endure one indignity after another.

Us DC loyalists are basically like fans of the pre-2026 Knicks, or the pre-2004 Red Sox, or the pre-2016 Cavs—take your pick. I wouldn’t even call myself so hardcore, but those were the guys I grew up on, especially as more of a Saturday morning cartoon-watcher than a comics reader. Bruce Timm’s Batman and Superman animated series, the way those two shows dovetailed to make Justice League while also charting bold new territory with Batman Beyond—that was my jam. It was also the era of incredible Fox shows like Spider-Man and X-Men, but never did I think those two would continue to thrive while auteur after auteur tried and failed to do what Timm accomplished before a legion of appreciative 11-year-olds.

It goes back to Wolfgang Peterson’s aborted Batman versus Superman film, a Hollywood sliding doors moment that created the conditions under which a young, hungry Christopher Nolan could prove his blockbuster mettle with Batman Begins and give the greatest hero to ever do it a well-deserved cinematic reset. As Nolan’s stock rose, Bryan Singer’s attempt to restore ‘70s vibes with Superman Returns flopped almost immediately, leaving DC in a Highlander situation yet again. The goodwill Nolan generated with his trilogy gave way to what we came to know as the Snyderverse, starting with Zack Snyder’s Superman reset Man of Steel, a solid film that I could never bring myself to love wholeheartedly.

Historians will tell you it was shareholder thirst to compete with Marvel that spelled doom for Snyder—and the pressure to shoehorn Batman, Wonder Woman and the rest of their squad in to fast-track a Justice League movie. His era certainly cultivated a base of devoted, even rabid stans who will attack anyone who besmirches their leader’s genius. But personally, I spent all of those years in a state of disbelief about the way some of the genre’s sturdiest, best and most crowd-pleasing characters were being subjected to all of this Frank Miller-reject vibes: ultra slo-mo, fight scenes of wanton and artless destruction, not to mention the Gal Gadot line-readings and Bruce Wayne mowing bad guys down in between crossfit sessions. The illest superhero team to do it, in the hands of a guy who saw Jared Leto and thought, “There’s a guy who can succeed Heath Ledger as an Oscar-worthy villain.” Snyder’s step-down from Justice League after a family tragedy and seeing his vision superimposed with Joss Whedon’s was very undignified. But The SnyderCut? Still not for me.

James Gunn’s residency was the most promising thing to happen to the Justice gang in a while, at least for those of us who don’t chug Mountain Dew and listen to Eminem all day. He was the first director in a long time to really, truly understand Superman’s throwback optimistic essence and successfully repackage that for a contemporary audience. Forget about the larger DC universe—what Gunn built in Metropolis alone felt like the beginning of a beautiful universe. Corenswet’s affable take on the character paired with his chemistry with Rachel Brosnahan had me even hoping Gunn would ease up on the big picture and just luxuriate in more Superman adventures. Still, even his slate could only be so fresh: he started in the shadow of Matt Reeves and Robert Pattinson’s The Batman, a critically acclaimed reboot that didn’t square with his vision. At best, we were going to be subjected to the indelicate circumstance of having two different Batmen in production at once. (And that Gunn thought highly enough of Andy Muschietti’s The Flash to tap him for DCU’s Batman film was concerning, for sure.)

But he was building something, and he wasn’t wasting time. Even before he understandably stepped away for a family emergency, Reeves was taking his sweet time to get The Batman II off the ground; Gunn launched his Superman last July and intended to drop a sequel, Man of Tomorrow, next July, one that likely would’ve built up to a Justice League film a little more gracefully than Snyder was allowed to. He may have been indulging side quests a little too freely, green-lighting things like a spin-off series for Skyler Gisondo’s Jimmy Olsen, but his focus on the main play at hand never wavered. The narrative that he was meandering was always in bad faith; look no further than Superman's first act, which breathlessly goes about establishing the status quo of Gunn’s DCU at times to the script’s detriment.

We were already seeing those seeds planted: this past summer’s Lanterns series on HBO, for instance, through which Aaron Pierre managed to turn John Stewart into something closer to a household name hero. (Pierre and Adria Arjona, who is most likely playing Wonder Woman, were set to appear in Man of Tomorrow.) Gunn’s quippy, vibrant vision may not have been for everyone, but he at least deserved the chance to cook a little bit longer. In a weird way, Gunn’s firing feels like one of the first pushbacks to the midterms blue wave. Looking for politics in comic book fare is ultimately asinine, but there’s a reason Superman 2025 was one of the most meme'd movies during the post November 3rd wave of optimism, to say nothing of the movie's plot being a paper-thin allegory for Israel and Palestine.

So what happens now? Who knows. Man of Tomorrow might be released as a sort of post-mortem, or it could be shelved altogether. Does David Corenswet go the way of Brandon Routh? Have we seen the last of this iteration of John Stewart? Will Adria Arjona’s Wonder Woman even get off the ground?

We’re back to square one. Skydance head David Ellision has already replaced Gunn and Safran with ex-MCU producer Jeremy Latcham, a guy who’s more concerned about making movies that’ll play for meemaw, peepaw and the reverend. It appears he'll be a down-the-middle role player who can serve up the most basic, populist take on all of these adaptations. I’m giving up on ever seeing a coherent, let alone genuinely great take on this squad of heroes. Many have tried, all have failed, and the people in charge have only gotten dumber. Go with God, DC faithful. We’ll always have the Bruce Timm cartoons.

#6641. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6640. Can a Silver Fanatic Be Convinced to Go for Gold?

There are some corners of fashion that continue to be very polarizing. Maybe you are a skinny jean or baggy jean devotee; A staunch believer in crewnecks, or V-necks; Or maybe you only exclusively carry itty-bitty mini bags, or huge maxi bags. But as the holiday season approaches, and festive parties are beginning to fill up your social calendar, the need for a perfectly-glitzy outfit brings up one of the most contentious debates of all: Are you team silver, or team gold?

Metallics, after all, are a pillar of holiday style. Whether it’s a shimmering gown, or a bejeweled shoe or statement earring, dressing for the season’s holiday parties is the perfect moment to shine bright—literally. Only problem is, picking a metallic can swiftly divide a room. Admit it: You’re either steadfastly choosing disco ball-worthy silvers, or decking yourself out in gorgeous, glimmering golds. There is virtually no in between. (Except maybe rose gold fans—but those are like spotting a unicorn in the wild.)

I, myself, have been a longtime silver fanatic. There’s something about an icy, chrome-like piece that has always paired better with my mostly-black, slightly rock ‘n’ roll wardrobe. A silver-sheen boot or chunky silver necklace? It feels sleek and edgy, just like my preferred clothing style. Golds feel too cheery and summery! And I’m not alone: I polled some of my Vogue colleagues for their thoughts on the enduring silver-versus-gold debate, and found many were in favor of cool tones, too.

“I have never and would never wear anything gold,” says senior Vogue editor Corey Seymour. “Gold just seems so look-at-me, while silver is (relatively) restrained and subdued. My Brooklyn-Italian wife is very pro-gold, but we've agreed to disagree.” Max Berlinger, Vogue Runway’s senior fashion news editor, agrees with the anti-gold rhetoric. “Because it's a bit more low-key, I think you can buy chunkier pieces,” he says of his precious silver staples. “I have a silver curb-link bracelet that I wear every day from Tiffany & Co, and even though it's a bigger piece, the silver makes it feel casual. I would never wear the same thing in gold.”

But the recent spring 2027 runways would beg to differ. The newest designer collections went all-in on gold: Saint Laurent’s Anthony Vaccarello designed a whole collection in the sunny metallics, sending items down the runway such as foiled trench coats and dainty stiletto sandals to match. Labels like Ralph Lauren showed gold pleated slip dresses, while Dolce & Gabbana went all in on 1980s maximalism with its chunky gold accessories. Sorry, diehard silver lovers (myself included), but the message of the season is clear: It’s officially time to go for gold.

As the outfit planning for this year’s holidays begins, then, I began wondering: Can I convince myself to actually switch it up? To trade in my comfort-zone silvers for something a little more glamorous and gilded?

Even as someone who has long avoided wearing gold, I can see the pros: There is an undeniable allure to the eye-catching hue. It feels just a little more opulent and bold, two adjectives that are perfect for holiday dressing. It also looks especially luxe when styled with a sleek black satin or leather look (like the Schiaparelli show did, with those huge golden sculptural necklaces)—and that’s how I traditionally wear my silvers. So, maybe going gold is not that much of a stretch after all.

In the past, another main fear with embracing gold has been that it’s all wrong for my coloring—that it leans far too warm for someone who reads more, well, pale—but as the recent catwalks have shown, there is actually versatility in shades of gold. You can do a deep Saint Laurent gold, or a lighter, almost beige-like Brunello Cucinelli gold. You can make gold work for you.

The same goes with one’s styling approach: You don’t have to deck yourself out in head-to-toe gold, like Saint Laurent. You can simply pick one golden hero piece, like a great investment boot or earring, and it will still have that same upbeat, decadent feel. And isn’t that how you want to feel at a holiday bash? Decadent! Not subtle!

Some of my Vogue co-workers agree that gold is super easy to incorporate into one’s wardrobe, and actually works as a year-round color trend—not just for the office Christmas party. “It looks so much better against skin in my opinion,” says Vogue’s vice president of marketing, Dana Mendelowitz. “Also, hate to state the obvious, but gold is more expensive. And there is a reason people say ‘good as gold’—not silver!”

Senior Vogue beauty and wellness editor Margaux Anbouba has even been told by a professional color analyst that she should be wearing more silver tones—but she won’t have any of that. She’s all in on gold, 365 days a year. “When I had my season assessed with The Color Guru, she said I was a Moonlit Winter, and it came with some troubling news: I should be wearing silver and white gold,” says Anbouba. “After a lifetime of dedication to yellow gold, I simply chose to ignore this part of the guidelines. Yes, I have added more shades of magenta, sapphire, and lime into my closet—but I draw the line at silver.”

Clearly, there are strong feelings on this matter—and it all comes down to personal preferences—but dipping into the world of gold is not nearly as scary a proposition that I once thought it was. But hear me out: Perhaps you don’t even have to choose a metallic. If you’re still on the fence, a few looks on the runways this season have made the case for mixed-metallic dressing—combining both silvers and golds into one eye-catching look. At Thom Browne, a silvery coat-dress had a golden sewn-in panel along the front; At Fforme, a glossy pair of silver trousers had an iridescent gold finish, depending on the way it caught the light.

Come December, though, you can certainly consider me influenced to embrace gold on its own. But I plan on making the golds work for me—like rocking this Sacrd Thndr bolo tie with gold accents, which falls perfectly in line with my western sensibility. Maybe one day I will even work myself up to rocking a full-on gilded glamour look, Saint Laurent-style. But only if I can somehow miraculously wake up and look like Hailey Bieber and Zoe Kravitz, that is.

#6638. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6637. Denis Villeneuve Talks ‘Dune: Part Three’ and Rebooting James Bond: ‘We Cannot F*ck It Up.’

“I’m out of a job,” Denis Villeneuve said, jokingly. Hours earlier, Villeneuve had signed off on the IMAX 70-milimeter print of Dune: Part Three, officially wrapping post-production on that film—and in turn, a decade-long chapter of the Quebecois writer-director’s working life.

Fresh off this milestone, Villeneuve and GQ had come to the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles for a conversation and a private screening of Dune: Part Two, presented by OMEGA, in honor of his anointment as GQ’s Director of the Year. Global Editorial Director Adam Baidawi introduced Villeneuve before the director and GQ’s Zach Baron dove into a conversation that covered his original Dune plans, where Dune: Part Three breaks from its predecessors, and Villeneuve’s feelings about taking over the James Bond franchise.

GQ’s Adam Baidawi and Zach Baron with Denis Villeneuve

“I feel light,” the director of the year told Baron, then added, “Numb.” He was still processing Dune’s end, he said—while also coming to grips with closing the book on “the most rewarding, inspiring, and best ten years of my life as a filmmaker.”

Villeneuve’s first two Dune films have raked in more than a billion dollars at the box office. Part Three appears likely to nearly double that when it hits theaters (and locks up most of the world’s IMAX screens) a week before Christmas. But at one point during his conversation with Baron, the director pushed back gently on the notion of these movies as a “franchise.”

“There was nothing industrial in the way they were made,” Villeneuve said. They were the work of “a bunch of friends”—a familial crew, out in the desert putting things together.

“In French,” the Quebecois director continued, “there is a word—artisanal. They are very personal. Made with a lot of care. They’re little big things—but in a way, they are delicate.”

After all, as sprawling and cosmically grand as they are, these movies are also a deeply personal project for the director, born of images that took root in his head when he first read Frank Herbert’s thick-as-a-brick, notoriously adaptation-resistant 1965 novel Dune at age 13. Later, as Villeneuve racked up credits and clout, people would ask him what his dream project was; the answer was always Dune.

“I kept saying to myself, Someone else will do it one day,” he told Baron. “Another filmmaker will adapt this book again. And I kept waiting, and I kept waiting, until I felt ready to do it myself.”

Herbert wrote five escalatingly bonkers Dune sequels before his death in 1986, but Villeneuve intended to walk away from the table after adapting the first book across two films.

“Trilogies are very dangerous,” he told Baron. “The first movie is a promise, and if you fulfill the promise with the second one, then there’s a feeling of security that comes with that, and you feel that you have a recipe…That’s the trap. Because then you repeat yourself.”

But after wrapping Part Two, Villeneuve found himself unable to stop thinking about Dune Messiah—the second Dune novel, which Herbert supposedly wrote in frustration, believing the audience had missed the point by embracing Paul Atreides as a hero.

Villeneuve said his take on Messiah is “a different beast” than the first two films, built it around the tension between Timothée Chalamet’s Paul and his Fremen consort Chani (Zendaya), who Villeneuve has re-imagined—in a pivotal departure from Herbert’s version—as a nonbeliever who takes a critical view of Paul’s rise to power.

Neel Shah, Timothy Simons, and Michael Lasker

Of course, the specter (S.P.E.C.T.R.E.?) of another franchise hung over the proceedings at the Lucas Museum. Villeneuve, after all, is only technically between jobs; he’s a self-described “monomaniac” who insists that he can only hyper-focus on one project at a time and has been locked in on Dune for a decade, but the as-yet-untitled 26th Bond film is in motion, with Villeneuve signed on to direct.

GQ’s Adam Baidawi, Denis Villeneuve, and OMEGA’s Lucien Jornod

He could say almost nothing in public about the project, or even when he’d begin shooting it—he joked about having “the target of the sniper” on his chest—but spoke of feeling the responsibility not to fail: “We cannot fuck it up. We do not have the choice.”

Over the past week, the casting rumors around Villeneuve’s Bond reboot have reached what our UK colleagues accurately termed the “fever-dream” stage. It might be Callum Turner or Slow Horses’ Jack Lowden, but it might be Robert Pattinson, who’s emerged as a surprise front-runner after months of supposition about the part being earmarked for a relative unknown. At some point, toward the end of Tuesday’s conversation, the subject of Bond 26’s lead could no longer be avoided.

“Has the role of James Bond been cast?” Baron asked the director.

“It’s—it’s in the process. In the process,” Villeneuve said with a smile. “I am pushing the gas.”

“Blink once for Robert Pattinson,” Baron suggested, “and twice for Callum Turner.”

Villeneuve, for the record, did not blink. ✦

GQ would like to thank Legendary Entertainment, Warner Bros., and Brianna Smith.
